POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:37:17 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Metsola tells MEPs not to rely on AI when drafting laws https://www.politico.eu/article/roberta-metsola-tells-meps-not-to-rely-on-ai-when-drafting-laws/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:35:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9270750 European Parliament President Roberta Metsola warned MEPs Wednesday not to be overreliant on AI in decision-making, as the Parliament prepares new guidelines for lawmakers on how to use it.

“Drafting an amendment with the help of AI cannot replace fundamentally the constructive debate with a colleague,” she said at an event on AI use in the Parliament. “Doing legal research with the help of AI cannot ultimately replace the judgment and the critical thinking needed to make a tough decision.”

Metsola said there must be “democratic accountability” in lawmaking and argued that “where AI is used, people should know.”

“No matter how AI may be used in a parliament, the responsibility is still [with] those who are elected,” she said.

Secretary-General Alessandro Chiocchetti said at the same event that Parliament is building its own AI tool for sensitive work, hosted on its internal infrastructure.

As POLITICO reported in July, commercial AI models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Meta’s Llama, can still be used for less sensitive tasks.

Parliament officials have warned of a surge in AI-written amendments, including some that reference laws that don’t exist. Chiocchetti cited the case of an MEP who turned to AI for legal advice and got a wrong answer. “Our jurists took two days just to prove ChatGPT wrong,” he said.

The administration will submit new guidelines on using AI to senior leaders “very soon,” Chiocchetti said. Existing guidelines for staff date from 2024.

“Basically it boils down to three things: be open about using artificial intelligence, meaning if they use it, they have to say it as the rules require; never put sensitive material into a public tool; and check everything before it leaves your desk because it is your name on it,” Chiocchetti said.

He added he wants to use AI to help sort through thousands of amendments. But the drafting and consideration of laws need to remain with MEPs, as “the risk is indeed that we delegate the political debate to a chatbot.”

“Every text we vote has to be one that people wrote, checked, and are willing to defend. Anyone reading a new regulation should be able to find out who decided and hold them responsible.”

]]> en Fridge hacks also hit French blood banks https://www.politico.eu/article/fridge-hacks-hit-french-blood-banks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:37:30 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9270216 France’s blood collection service confirmed that its refrigerators were hit by cyberattacks at the same time as supermarket fridges across the EU — though blood supplies were not affected.

The French Blood Establishment said Tuesday that monitoring and control systems for cold storage rooms deployed at three of its sites were affected, with temperature and defrosting thresholds raised to “very high levels.”

It was not the direct target of the cyberattacks and no blood samples or products were compromised, the EFS said. 

The incident appears linked to a fresh wave of cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators across Europe, which forced stores to throw out spoiled food. That wave came just weeks after French supermarkets were first hit by a cyberattack that also hit refrigerators.

French media reports said refrigeration company Coolworld is the supplier to EFS. The company said in a statement that it’s aware of the incident and that it “concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld.” It said only a “limited number” of its units were affected.

In the attacks on supermarkets, refrigerator defrost settings were manipulated so the coolers reached very high temperatures, mirroring the EFS’s experiences. The blood stored in the affected equipment, which included plasma bags for transfusions, has been “transferred or secured,” the EFS said.

French digital minister Anne Le Hénanff said in the country’s Senate today that the recent attacks on the country’s refrigerators “have directly targeted our economy and our supply chain.”

“I would even go so far as to say that, beyond that, their objective may potentially be to undermine the unity of our country and to create anxiety among the population,” she said.

Emile Marzolf contributed to this report.

The trilateral meeting would take place during the APEC summit hosted by China in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19, which the three leaders are expected to attend.

“China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in a press briefing.

Mao did not elaborate on which topics the leaders would cover if they convene, amid fears in Europe that talks on ending the war in Ukraine could take place without Kyiv or European capitals at the table.

Trump last month indicated interest in discussing “denuclearization” in a trilateral meeting, but “not so much” Ukraine. China hasn’t commented on what would be on the agenda, although German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Xi rejected the idea of discussing Ukraine in that format when both leaders spoke last week. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that such a meeting would be “appropriate and very useful,” but did not elaborate on a potential agenda.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed concern over a potential trilateral meeting, “I really don’t want this to be a ‘Yalta – 2, 3, 4,’ when there is a redistribution of influence,” Zelenskyy told reporters in late October, referring to the 1945 talks between the U.S., British and Soviet leaders to discuss the future of postwar Germany.

“Europe must and wants to play a role in this process,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Tuesday alongside Zelenskyy in Berlin. “Key elements of a peaceful solution — whether regarding sanctions or the security architecture — can only be resolved with us Europeans. And everyone involved knows that very well.”

]]> de Pistorius verteidigt Bevorzugung der deutschen Industrie bei Rüstungsausgaben https://www.politico.eu/article/pistorius-verteidigt-bevorzugung-der-deutschen-industrie-bei-ruestungsausgaben/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:47:02 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9269961 BERLIN – Verteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius hat Kritik zurückgewiesen, Deutschland stelle seine Rüstungsindustrie über die europäische Verteidigungszusammenarbeit. Deutschland wolle diese Zusammenarbeit und agiere nicht anders als andere Länder, sagte der SPD-Politiker am Mittwoch bei der Berliner Sicherheitskonferenz.

Pistorius reagierte damit auf Kritik von Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (FDP). Die Vorsitzende des Verteidigungsausschusses des EU-Parlaments, hatte Deutschland vorgeworfen, sich zu sehr auf Waffen deutscher Hersteller zu konzentrieren, statt mit europäischen Partnern zusammenzuarbeiten.

„Alle sagen einstimmig und jeden Tag – nicht nur sonntags –, dass wir mehr Zusammenarbeit im Verteidigungsbereich und mehr gemeinsame Rüstungsprojekte wollen“, sagte Pistorius. „Aber wenn es hart auf hart kommt, sagt jedes Land ebenso einstimmig, aber jeder für sich: ‚Meine Industrie darf nicht ins Hintertreffen geraten.‘“

Der Streit verdeutlicht ein Problem für Europas Ambitionen. Die EU-Staaten wollen stärkere Streitkräfte aufbauen und dafür mehr gemeinsam beschaffen, doch die Regierungen sind auch bestrebt, Arbeitsplätze und Fabriken im eigenen Land zu schützen.

Das zeigen auch die Zahlen. 2025 gaben die EU-Länder 115 Milliarden Euro für militärische Ausrüstung aus. Laut der Europäischen Verteidigungsagentur entfielen 24 Prozent dieser Ausgaben auf gemeinsame Beschaffungen.

Brüssel möchte, dass dieser Anteil bis 2030 mindestens 40 Prozent erreicht. Die EU hat das mit 150 Milliarden Euro dotierte SAFE-Programm für Waffenkredite ins Leben gerufen, um Länder zu bewegen, Waffen gemeinsam statt einzeln zu kaufen.

Doch Regierungen zögern oft, große Rüstungsaufträge an Unternehmen in anderen Ländern zu vergeben. Die polnische Regierung erklärte, sie wolle 89 Prozent der fast 44 Milliarden Euro, die sie aus dem SAFE-Fonds erhält, für die heimische Industrie ausgeben.

Pistorius verteidigte diesen Ansatz. Regierungen hätten auch eine Verantwortung dafür, ihre Volkswirtschaften und Industrien zu schützen.

„Ich würde daher die Kritik in Ihrer Frage zurückweisen“, sagte er zu Strack-Zimmermann. „Und wenn es Kritik zu üben gibt, dann sollte sie sich nicht gegen Deutschland richten, sondern gegen buchstäblich alle Europäer mit einer Rüstungsindustrie.“

Dieser Artikel erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

]]> de The blue tsunami sparks joy, hope and mockery in Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/us-midterm-election-democrats-blue-tsunami-hope-mockery-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:42:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9269262 Europe is feeling more than a little bit of schadenfreude.

In a stunning U.S. midterm election, Democrats regained control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, as well as several governorships, winning big in Republican strongholds like South Carolina, Texas and even Kansas. While some races were yet to be called Wednesday morning, the result is a monumental rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump.

For Europe, which has weathered Trump’s incessant verbal attacks and tariff threats for the last two years, it was a rare ray of hope in transatlantic politics — if not because Washington would become a more predictable partner, then at least because the U.S. president might be too distracted to focus his usual ire on Europeans.

European Parliament Vice President Sophie Wilmès, a former Belgian prime minister, heralded a “major shift in the balance of power in the U.S. Congress,” adding: “I hope it will lead to a calmer, more constructive relationship with Europe.”

It remains to be seen how Trump will shift his stance on Europe, if at all, with Congress no longer under his control. As president, he still retains many of the executive’s powers on foreign policy.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius called the Democratic victory “historic” but cautioned against Europe expecting too much. “We will seek close contact with the Democrats,” he said Wednesday morning at the Berlin Security Conference. “But we do not know what the president will do after the election in the near future.”

Two senior EU figures — both regular Trump antagonists — couldn’t resist celebrating the result, though.

“American society voted against policies that only impoverish,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate change denial and against the privileges of the elites.”

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski reshared his own tweet from June last year responding to Elon Musk, a key Trump ally. “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought,” he snarked.

Headache for Europe’s far right

For Europe’s ascendant far right, which has long balanced admiration for Trump with the reality that he is deeply unpopular across the continent, the midterms are an uncomfortable reminder of the political risks of being too closely associated with the U.S. president.

Jordan Bardella, leader of France’s National Rally (RN), was keen to chalk up Trump’s “unfavorable” result to his decision to go to war with Iran more than anything else.

“It’s the case that the U.S. intervention in Iran has had a very strong impact on the U.S. economy, but also on the European economy,” he said Wednesday morning.

Bardella added that the RN’s presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was still leading in the French polls ahead of next year’s election and insisted defeats for nationalist politicians in Brazil, Hungary and now the U.S. did not bode ill for his party’s chances.

But the cost-of-living crisis was top of American voters’ minds, according to polls. That’s also the case in European countries, from France to Spain to Greece, which are grappling with soaring rents and widespread anger at apparently impotent governments.

Marine Tondelier, leader of France’s Greens, said Trump had “made the United States the laughingstock of the world” and called the result a “warning for France” ahead of the presidential election in April.

“If our country brings the RN to power next year, it will meet the same tragic fate as the United States,” she said.

U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker sought to downplay the prospect of a shift in Washington’s foreign policy following the midterm elections, insisting that the issues facing the U.S. and its European allies remained unchanged.

“The foreign policy of the United States has not changed,” Whitaker said, adding that “the issues that we’re facing as a country and as an alliance are the same.”

European markets, meanwhile, greeted the results with cautious optimism. Paris, London and Frankfurt opened slightly higher on Wednesday, following the Democrats’ sweeping victory.

Reality check for Trump

For all the celebrations, European officials were also quick to acknowledge that a Democratic-controlled Congress does not automatically translate into a more accommodating U.S. administration.

Trump retains considerable room to maneuver on foreign policy, including on the issues that have most strained transatlantic ties: European security, trade and Russia’s war in Ukraine.

France’s Economy Minister Roland Lescure noted Wednesday morning that while Trump would be “quite weakened” domestically, the “unpredictable” president remained “in charge of international policy.”

But a hostile Congress could make it harder for him to push through his domestic agenda, while opening the door to greater scrutiny of his administration.

“Voters have a habit of balancing power,” Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola said on X, “and now the president’s hands are more tied in domestic and foreign policy.”

Former Italian Prime Minister Enrico Letta was more emphatic.

“Europe is much stronger” thanks to the “blue wave,” he wrote on X.

Kathleen Van Brempt, vice-chair of the European Parliament’s International Trade Committee, shared a White House tweet predicting a Trump victory — and captioned it that it was, actually, America that won.

“And he lost,” she said.

Despite the ballot-box drubbing, Trump himself couldn’t resist a final shot at Europe, during an election night call with Fox News.

“You look at Europe, it’s dying. You look at what’s going on in France, what’s going on in Italy and all these other countries. I mean, they’re going through a terrible time. And they may not even survive, frankly,” he warned. “And we are thriving.”

Cuerpo, who is also the country’s first deputy prime minister, “has shown huge management skills” in the current legislature, Sánchez said in an address.

Cuerpo has been a rising figure in Sánchez’s government. A technocrat who served as secretary general of the Treasury under Nadia Calviño while she was economy minister, he took over her portfolio when she was elected to lead the European Investment Bank. Sánchez later promoted him to be his first deputy.

Puente resigned on Tuesday over the Oct. 28 train crash in Toledo province that killed 69 people, calling his decision “a matter of political dignity.” It was Spain’s second deadly rail disaster this year after January’s accident in Adamuz, which killed 46 people.

“With his resignation, Óscar is contributing to Spain gaining back its confidence not only in our railway system, but also in political dignity,” Sánchez said.

]]> en Defense chief rejects claims Germany puts its own arms industry ahead of Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/pistorius-rejects-claims-germany-puts-its-own-arms-industry-ahead-of-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:05:02 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9269301 BERLIN — German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Wednesday pushed back against criticism that Berlin is putting its own arms industry ahead of European defense cooperation, arguing that other countries are doing exactly the same.

Speaking at the Berlin Security Conference, Pistorius was responding to Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, chair of the European Parliament’s defense committee, who accused Germany of remaining too focused on buying weapons from its own manufacturers instead of working with European partners.

“Everyone says, unanimously and every day, not just on Sundays, that we want more defense cooperation and more joint armament projects,” Pistorius said. “But when push comes to shove, every country says, just as unanimously, but each for itself: ‘My industry must not be left behind.’”

The dispute highlights a major problem for Europe’s defense ambitions. EU countries want to build stronger armed forces and buy more weapons together, but governments are also keen to protect jobs and factories at home.

The numbers show how difficult that cooperation remains. EU countries spent €115 billion on military equipment in 2025, but only 24% of that spending went toward joint purchases, according to the European Defence Agency.

Brussels wants that share to reach at least 40% by 2030. The EU has also launched the €150 billion SAFE loans-for-weapons program to encourage countries to buy arms together rather than separately.

But national interests continue to get in the way, with governments often reluctant to see major weapons contracts go to companies in other countries. Poland’s government said it wants 89% of the almost €44 billion it is getting in SAFE funds to be spent on domestic industries.

Pistorius defended that approach, saying governments also have a responsibility to protect their economies and industries.

“I would therefore reject the criticism in your question,” he told Strack-Zimmermann. “And if there is criticism to be made, it should not be directed at Germany, but at literally all Europeans with a defense industry.”

He doled out around $446 million — the most a non-candidate has ever spent on an election, including over $200 million on Texas-related efforts. Musk’s preferred candidates across the country were swamped, losing almost everywhere, including Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race and Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio gubernatorial race.

His plans for a buildout of data centers across Texas are especially in doubt after Democrat Gina Hinojosa won a surprise victory over incumbent Greg Abbott in the state’s gubernatorial race.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X on Wednesday morning, jumping off the results to boost an idea he’s trying to pursue.

He quickly followed that with a joke about election interference, writing, “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

Musk’s adopted home of Texas has been a hot spot for data centers and data center construction over the last couple of years, with Abbott a strong ally of both tech leaders and Wall Street.

“Amid data center backlash all across the country, Texas was supposed to be an AI oasis, where people would be able to build data centers no matter what was happening in the rest of America,” said Sam Koppelman, the publisher of Hunterbrook Media — an investigative journalism outlet connected to a hedge fund. “This election totally changed that.”

With Democrats taking control of the U.S. Congress, Musk may also be a target for a party looking to pillory tech CEOs — with some Democrats pushing to bring tech CEOs in front of Congress.

“Voters rejected Republicans in part because they were bought and paid for by AI billionaires,” Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas said in a statement on Tuesday evening. “Democrats must hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:53:47 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 [Interview] ‘It’s now or never’ for enlargement, Montenegro’s former EU ambassador warns https://euobserver.com/246762/interview-its-now-or-never-for-enlargement-montenegros-former-eu-ambassador-warns/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:52:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246762 "With the Russian intervention in Ukraine, the geopolitical situation changed dramatically ... the EU understood they have to fortify 'their territory' in south-eastern Europe, and now you have, again, full energy [in the enlargement process]," Bojan Šarkić said.]]> If internal EU politics were to block Montenegro’s accession in 2028, it would risk killing Western Balkans enlargement and leaving a “black hole” in Europe, a veteran diplomat from Podgorica told EUobserver.

“I’m afraid it’s now or never,” said Bojan Šarkić, former Montenegro ambassador to the EU from 2016 to 2020.

“If it doesn’t happen, that would be a very bad signal to everyone in the region. The reaction would be: ‘Look at these Montenegrins. They did everything they were asked to do by the EU and what did they get? Nothing’,” he added.

“It would confirm what eurosceptics in the region have been saying – and there are quite a few of them. Just switch on Serbian TV, every day you hear: ‘The EU is falling apart. Look at the demonstrations in France’,” he said.

“And all this creates fertile soil for interference by other countries,” Šarkić said, referring to Russia.

The 67-year-old diplomat, who retired last year, spoke to EUobserver as the European Commission prepared to publish its annual reports on the 10 candidate countries in line to join the 27-nation bloc one day – the six Western Balkan states, Georgia, Moldova, Turkey, and Ukraine.

Šarkić began his diplomatic career in the former Yugoslavia in 1987, spent four years in Moscow in what was then the Soviet Union, before being sent to London and Brussels.

Croatia was the last country to join the EU, in 2013.

Following the EU’s migration crisis in 2015, enlargement appetite waned, while Turkey’s post-coup crackdown in 2016 saw its talks put on hold.

In the past two years, democratic backsliding in Georgia and Serbia also saw their talks frozen.

But at the same time, Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022 created a new geopolitical imperative to save the Western Balkans and post-Soviet states from becoming what Šarkić called a “black hole” of instability and Russian meddling in Europe.

The EU fast-tracked Moldova and Ukraine’s accession bids, while Armenia also peeled away from Russia and now aimed to formally apply for membership, in 2027 or 2028.

“In my time in Brussels, I had top politicians in the EU, in the Council, in the European Commission, telling me to forget about becoming a member of the EU in the forthcoming future,” said Šarkić.

“And while the EU was slow and lazy on enlargement, Russia was not lazy at all in trying to build its influence in the region,” he said.

]]> Roma ‘intimidation’ in Bulgarian presidentials as Iliana Iotova’s win raises alarm bells for press freedom https://euobserver.com/246567/roma-intimidation-in-bulgarian-presidentials-as-iliana-iotovas-win-raises-alarm-bells-for-press-freedom/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:28:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246567 Iliana Iotova's election win in Bulgaria's presidential run-off has analysts worried about her relationship with Russia and attitude towards democratic freedoms. She is expected to align with prime minister Rumen Radev.]]> Bulgaria’s Iliana Iotova’s presidential run-off win came after an election fraught with heavy policing of Roma voters and warning signs for the country’s media ecosystem.

Her victory in Sunday’s poll has strengthened Bulgaria’s pro-Russian stance, building on the success of Rumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria party in the April 2026 parliamentary elections, analysts say.

Bulgarian Socialist Party candidate Iotova won 57.6 percent of votes against pro-European independent Andrey Gyurov’s 39.5 percent in Bulgaria’s presidential election run-off.

She first became president in January when her predecessor Radev successfully ran for prime minister in a snap election.

Roma ‘intimidation’ amid low turn-out

Iotova won the Bulgarian presidency with the lowest number of votes of a presidential election winner in decades. 

“There are many voters who abstain from voting, because they don’t see any of the promises of Progressive Bulgaria being fulfilled,” Vesselin Zhelev, the foreign desk editor of media outlet Club Z, told EUobserver.

“Many Radev supporters have become disappointed that he didn’t do good on his promises to fight inflation or to take meaningful steps against corruption and oligarchy or for judicial reform,” he added. 

Read more

[Interview] Bulgaria’s presidential election becomes a test of Rumen Radev’s grip on power

And turnout among Roma people, an ethnic minority of up to 10 percent of Bulgaria’s population, also hit record lows amid reports of police intimidation of the community at polling stations.

Adela Militaru, programme director at the Barcelona-based political foundation Roma for Democracy, said candidates’ lack of an agenda for Roma people is “politically dumb”. As a result, she said, Roma voters have “unseen” abstention rates.

Militaru’s organisation described police being stationed outside polling stations in Roma neighbourhoods, and counted 175 to 180 police raids in voting locations during the first round of the presidential election.

The reports come amid a history of vote-buying in the country and antigypsyism across Europe.

Militaru said the police raids “intimidate voters” and “stigmatise the Roma rather than dismantling broker networks operating on the ground”.

She added that Bulgarian politicians have not made visible attempts to garner support from the Roma community: “The Roma vote can actually be won by anyone who wants to compete for it.”

“The current political offer remains extremely limited towards Roma voters. Future political offers should include housing and land, education and employment, support for Roma entrepreneurship, culture and identity,” Militaru also said.

‘Alarm bells’ raised for media

Iotova was a TV news chief before entering politics, serving a seven-year stint as a member of the European Parliament. Her vice-president Kiril Valchev is stepping down as head of the National Telegraph Agency.

Teodora Yovcheva, a political scholar at Sofia University, told EUobserver she is worried that ties between the government and media could be influencing press freedom.

]]> Listen: What is Europe’s military exercise in Poland really for? https://euobserver.com/246745/listen-what-is-europes-military-exercise-in-poland-really-for/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 09:19:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246745 A large-scale military exercise is about to begin in Poland, starting Monday, 9 October. The coalition of the willing is testing how their forces work together and sending a political message supporting Ukraine.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

A large-scale military exercise is about to begin in Poland, starting next week. It will last more than ten days and bring together 11 countries.

So what is this exercise really for? The exercise is an initiative of the “coalition of the willing”, a group of around thirty countries. This is not NATO and this is important. It’s a group of countries that have volunteered to act, outside of any binding framework.

Only eleven of them are taking part in the exercise because of time constraints. France is providing the bulk of the contingent, alongside the United Kingdom, Belgium and Poland, among others.

Read more

THIS WEEK: EU enlargement report tops Brussels agenda as ‘coalition of the willing’ faces Trump’s midterm test

So what will these 2,800 troops actually be doing for more than ten days? Its goal is to test, and to show, what Europeans are actually able to do as part of security guarantees for Ukraine.

Let’s maybe remember what we mean by “security guarantees”. These are the commitments some European countries are ready to make once the war is over, or at least after a genuine ceasefire, to make sure Ukraine is not invaded again.

Ukraine insists on this for a simple reason: the Minsk agreements of 2015, meant to bring peace to the Donbas, were never respected by Russia.

Back to the exercise. Troops will be testing command structures, logistics and, above all, coordination between air, naval and land forces. The ground exercise takes place in Poland, the aircraft are expected to fly in from Romania, and Turkey should lead a simulated maritime exercise.

According to Tom Bateman, the commander of this exercise, the aim is to show that this contingent can be deployed quickly. And of course, it’s also a signal to Kyiv: the volunteer countries are serious when they promise security guarantees.

Read more

[Interview] There are still more American soldiers than Western ones on Nato’s eastern border, says defence expert Robert Pszczel

But there is another message, aimed at Washington. The American contribution to these guarantees is, for now, completely uncertain, just like the US support for Ukraine’s war effort more broadly.

So Europeans are playing on two fronts. First, setting an example, and perhaps encouraging the Americans to join in, or at least to provide a safety net. And second, simply getting ready to manage without them. A full-scale exercise helps with that.

Now, is it already settled that Ukraine can count on European troops on its soil once the war is over? Yes and no. At the EU level, there are commitments in that regard, but the term “security guarantees” is broad and could cover different things: It could be men, but it could also be material support only. All of this is not clear.

France and the United Kingdom, however, have gone further. In a declaration of intent signed in January, they committed to sending forces to Ukraine if a peace deal is reached. Emmanuel Macron has even spoken of “several thousand soldiers”.

Read more

Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

But France is far from having unanimous support, whether within the EU or within NATO. And for good reason: European troops potentially facing Russian soldiers would risk opening a new conflict.

That’s why the ideas on the table always refer to preventive forces, deployed far from the front line.

Finally, as far as the peace negotiations are concerned, a trilateral meeting between Russia, Ukraine and the United States is planned next week in Abu Dhabi.

Ahead of that, an American delegation is in Brussels this week to prepare the ground with the Europeans, who are not part of the talks in Abu Dhabi.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was in Berlin yesterday.
In his own words, it was about diplomatic coordination, strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and supporting its energy sector.

Let’s see whether this show of force in Poland is enough to make European guarantees credible, in Kyiv, in Moscow and in Washington.

]]> It’s not a coup: Tusk is right to reclaim Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, but wrong in how he does it https://euobserver.com/246515/its-not-a-coup-tusk-is-right-to-reclaim-polands-constitutional-tribunal-but-wrong-in-how-he-does-it/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246515 Donald Tusk has a legal duty to rebuild Poland’s captured Constitutional Tribunal. But the government’s handling of the latest confrontation and its own appointments risks turning a victory for the rule of law into a political defeat, writes Alberto Alemanno.]]> Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal is at the centre of an unprecedented rule-of-law confrontation.

Last Friday (30 October), seven judges elected by parliament entered the court in a highly-contentious operation, escorted by the state protection service.

After more than six months of president Karol Nawrocki refusing to accept their oaths, one of them, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, announced she was assuming leadership of the tribunal.

Nawrocki cut short his official visit to Senegal and rushed back to Warsaw. Cameras filmed the scuffles at the entrance.

The images prompted two opposing interpretations: a legitimate effort to restore the rule of law, or a coup?

Whatever the images suggested, Friday’s operation was not a coup. It aimed to restore a lawful court, not to capture it.

Read more

[Explainer] Polish right turns court dispute into election battleground, dragging in the EU

Far-right seizes on spectacle

Yet the circumstances surrounding Friday’s intervention made that accusation easier to spread, as hard-right leaders from Marine Le Pen to Nigel Farage quickly showed.

The crisis began in December 2015, when Poland’s then-governing Law and Justice party (PiS) appointed three judges to seats that had already been filled.

What followed was a sustained effort to bring the country’s constitutional watchdog under political control. Its leadership became increasingly aligned with the political interests of the former ruling party, with its president, Julia Przyłębska, described as an ally of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Its rulings helped dismantle constitutional safeguards, most consequentially through its October 2020 decision restricting access to abortion.

European courts have also ruled on the Tribunal’s compromised composition and lack of independence.

Courts judge Tribunal

In December 2025, the European Union’s highest court ruled that Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal could not be considered an independent and impartial court established by law, citing irregularities in the appointment of some of its judges and its president.

The European Court of Human Rights had reached a similar conclusion in 2021. In May this year, it ordered Poland not to obstruct judges elected by parliament. The Council of Europe’s legal experts also made clear in October that the president cannot simply refuse to swear in judges chosen by the legislature.

On Saturday, the European Commission confirmed that the appointment of constitutional judges falls within parliament’s powers.

The law is clear: Poland must have an independent Constitutional Tribunal. By refusing to swear in judges elected by parliament, the country’s president is abusing his office to block their appointments and effectively claiming a veto power he does not have.

This constitutes a breach of – not a defence – of the rule of law. Yet the president’s obstruction does not give the government unlimited discretion in how it restores the tribunal. Its response must also comply with the law.

Friday’s operation raises legitimate questions.

]]> Is the Western Sahara now friendless? No, EU backing for Morocco is conditional, and Spanish election will be pivotal https://euobserver.com/246595/is-the-western-sahara-now-friendless-no-eu-backing-for-morocco-is-conditional-and-spanish-election-will-be-pivotal/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246595 Spain's general election could be, in part, a referendum on the country's partnership with Morocco, with the opposition promising tougher border control measures and closer ties with Rabat's neighbour and enemy, Algeria.]]> The collapse of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a 35 year mandate, is the latest diplomatic win for Morocco, but Rabat’s European support may prove to be less conclusive than it thinks. 

The end came at a UN Security Council last week, when the United States and Russia effectively cancelled each other out by vetoing rival resolutions on extending the mandate of the UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. 

Russia vetoed a US-drafted resolution on Western Sahara at the Security Council on Friday (30 October), leaving the UN peacekeeping mission without a renewed mandate just a day before it expired. 

The US resolution would have extended the mission for another year but enshrining a plan to give Western Sahara limited autonomy under Morocco’s sovereignty as the only basis ‌for talks to settle the dispute that dates back to the end of Spanish colonialism in the 1970s. The US text also proposed to remove any reference to a referendum among the Sahrawi people on their future. 

The security council then rejected a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission for a year. France and the UK — the two other permanent Security Council members — along with eight non-permanent members, backed the US resolution. 

The end of the UN mission is undeniably better for Morocco than the Polisario Front, the political wing of the Sahrawi independence movement.

]]> Czech public broadcasters hold historic strike following government vote to abolish license fees https://euobserver.com/246573/czech-public-broadcasters-hold-historic-strike-following-government-vote-to-abolish-license-fees/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:56:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246573 Thousand of Czechs joined public TV and radio workers in their walkout over the Czech government's moves to bring public broadcasting under its political control.]]> First published in Deník N.

A strike by workers of public TV and radio workers interrupted broadcasts and drew thousands of people onto the streets across the Czech Republic.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Prague, Brno and Ostrava demonstrations supported by media, students, theatres and more than 300 Czech athletes.

“An unprecedented day in the history of Czech public service media has begun”, said Michal Kubal, Czech Television’s news chief, at 00:00 on 3 November 2026 marking a start to an all-day strike by the broadcasting workers.

He read an opening statement from a sheet of paper during the midnight dispatch. “This broadcast will change. The midnight news is one of many programmes that will look completely different on Czech Television screens from what viewers are used to,” Daniel Stach said on air. The organiser of the strike appeared on TV with a darkened studio as backdrop.

Presenter Kubal went on to explain that staff at Czech Television and Czech Radio were using the one-day strike to fight for independence of both public service media outlets, in response to a government moves to scrap license fees and move public their funding to the state budget.

Read more

Czech government approves first step to scrapping TV and radio licence fees in 4.36am vote, sparking protests

TV management had concluded a memorandum with the strike organisers under which media staff would provide essential news coverage in the event of extraordinary developments.

“A large majority of women and men working at both media outlets have joined the strike. This afternoon, they will also take part in public gatherings in Prague and other cities in support of public service media,” Kubal added.

Those tuning into ČT24 could see a notice about the the public broadcaster’s news network minimalist provisional regime.

“Czech Television employees are on strike. We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue providing a public service in full and to the highest standard in the future,” the notice read.

A STEM/MARK survey for Czech Television says 68 percent of people of Czechs agree public service media should stay well away from state control or private ownership.

“Thank you for watching Czech Television — in times of crisis, at historically pivotal moments and on entirely ordinary weekdays,” said Stach, one of the leading figures of the Veřejnoprávně initiative, which called the strike, as he concluded the roughly five-minute midnight news bulletin.

]]> Firefighters from 19 countries protest EU budget cuts in Brussels https://euobserver.com/246651/firefighters-from-19-countries-protest-eu-disaster-budget-cuts-in-brussels/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:20:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246651 Around 1,000 firefighters from 19 countries gathered in Brussels Tuesday to demand more equipment, more staff, and adequate healthcare, only weeks before key EU budget negotiations.]]> Around 1,000 firefighters from 19 countries gathered in Brussels on Tuesday (3 November) to demand more equipment, more staff, and adequate healthcare, only weeks before key EU budget negotiations.

With wildfires growing bigger and more often due to climate change, there needs to be more professional firefighters, with modern equipment, to face them, argues the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), who organised the protest together with various Belgian workers’ organisations.

As of 7 October, 692 419 hectares burnt in wildfires across the EU this year – an area almost as big as the Greek island of Crete – burning some 30 million tonnes of CO2. Southern countries, Portugal, Greece, Italy, and Spain, suffered most. According to the World Health Organisation, wildfires in Europe have increased by 57 percent since 2022.

Read more

Europe’s summer of wildfires puts spotlight on economic cost of climate inaction

On average, wildfires cause some €2.5bn losses across the EU each year.

The protest gathered in front of a conference on civil protection organised by the EU Commission, where crisis management commissioner Hadja Lahbib presented new guidelines on what citizens should prepare for the first days of an emergency.

The firefighters and unions were there to protest the cuts to the next EU budget for disaster management: from over €10bn requested by the commission to just under €7bn proposed by the Irish presidency last month. Yet that would still be double what the 2021-2027 budget had room for.

“I believe that the risk is getting bigger. So yes, it’s necessary to also increase the support,” Tiago da Cunha, president of a municipality in northern Portugal, where the most summer wildfires hit in 2026, told EUobserver.

Read more

Europe’s 2026 wildfires show the cost of ignoring prevention

Stalo Yostili, 43, has been a firefighter in Cyprus for a decade. She said her country does not recognise how dangerous the profession is. She complained of too few staff, which means for an operation that would normally need 15 firefighters, only six are sent, making it more potentially dangerous.

Profession-specific healthcare is also a big topic, Ireneusz Kierzkowski from the Polish firefighter union, told EUobserver. Retired firefighters often have PTSD, and they also develop cancers more often.

]]> Microsoft cloud in Ireland under fire for hosting Israeli app used to monitor Palestinians in occupied West Bank https://euobserver.com/246599/microsoft-cloud-in-ireland-under-fire-for-hosting-israeli-app-used-to-monitor-palestinians-in-occupied-west-bank/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:49:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246599 Microsoft hosts key software used to monitor movements of Palestinians in the occupied West bank. Some of this is being hosted in Ireland. ]]> Microsoft software plays a key part in running an app used by Israel to control Palestinian mobility in the occupied territories, a new report found. 

Al Munasseq, meaning ‘The Coordinator’ in Arabic, is an app launched by Israel’s Coordination of Government Activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (COGAT) unit in 2019 to manage the movement of Palestinians for work, healthcare, prayer, and everyday tasks.

A report published on Tuesday (3 November) by global consumer group Ekō found Microsoft to be hosting key components of Al Munasseq in data centres in Ireland, effectively enabling what is feared to be mass surveillance.

The app runs on Microsoft’s Azure cloud and uses its cloud storage and database services. When someone uses the app, it’s Microsoft’s servers that process their request, and Microsoft that keeps those servers running so the app stays available.

“For Palestinians, Al Munasseq is the gatekeeper to ordinary life. A cancer patient who needs radiotherapy in Jerusalem, a worker who needs to feed his family, a daughter who wants to sit beside her mother in hospital – all of them must ask Israel’s military for a permit to move across their own stolen land, and that permission runs through the Al Munasseq app,” said Ekō senior campaign director, Rewan Al-Haddad.

Read more

EU risks funding Israeli firms which help develop NAZA-type violent tech

“If a Western tech giant can host the machinery powering apartheid in Ireland, inside the EU, and face no consequences, every other company will learn it can do the same,” Al-Haddad told EUobserver. 

Deputy Sinead Gibney, who serves on the Irish parliament’s AI committee, called for an investigation in light of the report findings.

    ]]>         Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government https://euobserver.com/246552/serbias-student-list-has-been-inspirational-but-the-big-test-will-be-forming-a-stable-anti-corruption-government/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:15:05 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246552 The Serbian campaign looked exceptional. I cannot think of many cases of an opposition that was so decentralised and so democratic internally. The closest comparison may be the early German Greens that had a strong Basisdemokratie ["Grassroots Democracy"] out of conviction; or the faceless and fluid democratic movement in Hong Kong ("Be Water") out of necessity. This is inspirational.]]> The ink had hardly dried under articles explaining lessons learned from Péter Magyar’s electoral overthrow of Hungary’s government, when Serbia’s Student List managed to overthrow the semi-authoritarian Aleksandar Vučić.

    Both cases had similarities: long-standing rulers that lied and flaunted their corruption ever more openly; they were ripe for defeat.

    In both cases the opposition avoided strongly partisan positioning and instead focused on state functioning and anti-corruption. 

    Intriguingly, they had almost identical results: 53 percent of the vote for the opposition, 39 percent for the incumbent party. In both cases the opposition showed unity and campaigned across the country and on social media; a well-known ingredient of any campaign to overthrow entrenched authoritarians. 

    Read more

    Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll

    In other ways the two cases are strikingly different.

    The Hungarian campaign was focused on Magyar, a consummate politician and former Fidesz member, who knew the incumbent party from the inside.

    In Serbia a collective of students from different universities turned massive mobilisation against the corrupt government into an electoral platform. 

    In Hungary, Magyar dominated his party, in Serbia, the student collective reached decisions democratically, voting on all major points; an extreme contrast between a one-man show and a movement that hardly had any individual faces. 

    What can we learn from these elections?

    First, we should not get fixated on silver bullets. One success story does not mean that the same recipe works elsewhere. Social movements and electoral campaigns are highly complex and contingent on circumstances. No leader like Magyar appeared in Serbia, no massive student initiative developed in Hungary, although both had similar problems of political repression by the ruling party.

Search-and-rescue ships have been hampered by legal hurdles and funding cuts, while the central Mediterranean has become a grave for tens of thousands of people.]]> Search-and-rescue NGO efforts to conduct life-saving work in the Mediterranean face continuous derailment by European authorities hoping to stop migrants reaching EU soil – and drowning thousands in the process.

    Since Friedrich Merz took over as German chancellor in May 2025, all funding to national search-and-rescue organisations has stopped. 

    The conservative leader has faced accusations from other EU leaders that the German NGO vessels prevalent across the central Mediterranean’s deadly zone of migrant crossings have acted as a ‘pull factor’, attracting migration to the EU.

    After rescuing 28 people adrift in an overcrowded dinghy last week, the humanitarian NGO has now in total rescued 5,213 people since August 2022. A third of those were children. 

    SOS Humanity were part of a former funding pool that split an annual €2m from Germany’s federal budget for humanitarian aid between search-and-rescue organisations. Despite growing fuel costs, and increasing legal costs from administrative barriers and port detentions by the Italian government, search-and-rescue groups are now dealing with an astronomical gap in their budget. 

    This has also been compounded since Giorgia Meloni’s far-right Italian government came into power in 2022.

    ]]>         When adults take over youth protests, EU children’s own demands vanish https://euobserver.com/246292/when-adults-take-over-youth-protests-eu-childrens-own-demands-vanish/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:25:18 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246292 As youth protests spread from France to Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece and Albania, Europe is confronting a stark test of whether under‑18s are treated as political actors in their own right, or merely as props in adult power struggles.]]> France’s lycée students have taken to the streets over shortages of teachers, crumbling buildings, and inequalities that determine educational opportunities and university admissions.

    Yet, as political parties and trade unions joined the protests and students found themselves confronted by riot police, the debate shifted from their demands to their inability to act for themselves.

    In France, adultism has deep roots, reflected in negative stereotypes of young people, their gradual exclusion from public spaces, and the persistent assumption that children are politically innocent and therefore easily manipulated by adults.

    Here lies a democratic paradox: children are expected to develop into politically responsible citizens, but when they start behaving like them, their political agency suddenly becomes questionable.

    Lost in this debate, however, is the fact that students are making political claims of their own, challenging not only their school conditions, but also the political decisions and budgetary priorities that perpetuate these inequalities and jeopardise their future.

    Read more

    Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting

    A right to speak, but who will listen?

    Beyond the political controversy, children are already political citizens, even without voting rights.

    The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by every state except the United States, guarantees freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly, and requires children’s views to be given due weight in matters affecting them.

    The EU and France also have legal provisions recognising children’s participation rights, including in educational governance.

    However, political citizenship extends beyond a formal legal status to participation in public life, where children can actively exercise political agency through expression, collective action, and political claims.

    Their exclusion from electoral politics does not diminish their political legitimacy, nor relieve states of their obligation to take their voices seriously.

    But can blockades and protests bring about the change children demand? Faced with  hundreds of thousands of demonstrators taking to the streets across France in support of students, the French government appears to have rediscovered the virtues of listening to children, launching consultations and promising stronger student representation, more teachers, and funding for school renovations.

    Student representatives welcomed some of these commitments, but insisted on seeing actual renovations and additional teachers in classrooms.

    With the 2027 presidential election approaching in France, these commitments risk becoming entangled in campaigning, and potentially overshadowing children’s demands with competing political agendas.

    The question is what will come of the promises; and just as importantly, who will be held accountable, and how, if those promises are never delivered?

    Read more

    Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate

    Adults arrive, children disappear?

    The growing involvement of adults (teachers, parents, unions) in the protests also fuelled accusations of political instrumentalisation: the government was quick to accuse left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) of manipulating the children.

    If there was any adult interference, it deserves scrutiny, but assuming that children must be manipulated whenever they organise politically is mere adultism disguised as paternalistic concern. 

    Concerns over the criminalisation of children’s protests have also grown. While incidents of vandalism and violence overshadowed students’ demands, the crackdown was striking: by 14 October, 6,773 minors had been taken into custody, with 2,190 of them facing prosecution.

    Children are apparently mature enough to face legal consequences, even as their political competence is questioned.

    Meanwhile, investigations into police violence against minors raise questions about the state’s duty to protect them.

    As the riots of 17 October erupted into violence and chaos, students’ demands seemed to have faded from sight amid an increasingly heated debate over public order and wider social and political tensions.

    Meanwhile, protests by young people have also taken place elsewhere in Europe, in Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece, and Albania.

    Although grievances and political circumstances differ, these protests reveal an important distinction between schoolchildren and university students as political citizens.

    Most university students can vote, allowing them to turn collective mobilisation into electoral pressure, as Serbia’s student-backed movement showed when it won the parliamentary election on 25 October.

    But most secondary-school pupils have no equivalent leverage: their political citizenship depends on adults and institutions taking their demands seriously, without constantly calculating how many votes they could win or lose. 

    Beyond the diverse political interpretations of these protests lies another important question: what will children themselves take away from these experiences, and how might these impact their political citizenship?

    They may seek greater influence through consultations, intensify protests or create alternative forms of participation.

    But if their demands continue to fall on deaf ears, while protesting exposes them to the threat of police repression and to adultism, disillusionment may instead drive some away from political participation altogether.

    The promise of children’s rights to be heard was certainly more ambitious than that.

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    Find the full transcript below:

    Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate. According to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.

    What would a Democratic win actually change for Europeans? First, a quick word on what to expect tonight. Polls suggest a win for the Democrats camp, especially in the House of Representatives. 

    It is actually common for the president’s party to lose ground at the midterms. And Donald Trump’s approval ratings have been falling steadily.

    So, if the Democrats do win, what could they do? Quite a lot, on paper at least. Congress holds significant powers. The House can, for instance, launch impeachment proceedings against the president. But removing him from office would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which is very hard to reach.

    The Democrats have said they would open investigations into the administration, including on corruption. They want to keep financial support for Ukraine in place, and to end the war in Iran. They also want to roll back many of the tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

    Read more

    THIS WEEK: EU enlargement report tops Brussels agenda as ‘coalition of the willing’ faces Trump’s midterm test

    These are all issues of great importance for Europe. But could the Democrats really undo them?

    For several of these issues, a simple majority is enough to pass a law. So on that front, they could take a stand. But there is a catch: the president has a veto.

    And to override this veto, Congress needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers. In the House, that means around 290 seats. And even in the most optimistic polls, the Democrats don’t get there.

    Those polls currently point to a tight race for the Senate, and a more comfortable Democratic win in the House.

    Of course, these are estimates to be taken with a pinch of salt. The BBC reminded us yesterday that polls in the United States regularly get it wrong, although they do so less often for midterms.

    Read more

    Trump, Rubio and Hegseth are fumbling Ukraine – Europe needs to stop making the same mistake

    In any case, a two-thirds majority looks like an unlikely scenario. Still, this doesn’t mean nothing will change. The Democrats would still have some levers if they do win.

    They could, for example, block bills by simply refusing to vote for them. And they could hold up the budget, and with it, the funding of the war effort.

    In the case of the tariffs, the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Donald Trump had overstepped his powers since Congress had not approved the tariffs. This is already a difficulty, even if, for now, the government is playing with the legal basis of the tariffs. 

    So, to sum up: the Democrats wouldn’t be able to overturn Donald Trump’s policies altogether, but they could make his life a lot harder.

    ]]>         Andrew Tate’s toxic legacy in Romania is warping its democracy https://euobserver.com/246239/andrew-tates-toxic-legacy-in-romania-is-warping-its-democracy/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:17:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246239 While prosecutors chase the Tates across borders, their macho fantasy of domination is already shaping how a frustrated generation of Romanian men sees women and democracy itself.]]> Prosecutors in Romania officially charged social media influencers Andrew and Christian Tate with trafficking and sex offences involving minors on 4 September. But the Tates were not around to be hauled into a police station in Bucharest – they were in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK on similar charges.

    That two of the world’s most high-profile misogynists may finally be brought to justice is a reason to celebrate. But in the country which hosted them for so many years, their toxic legacy continues to pollute the atmosphere.

    Why did the Tates choose Romania in the first place?

    Before his arrest Andrew Tate expressed a preference for countries where “corruption is accessible to everybody.” 

    An underregulated webcam industry and struggles with combating sex trafficking could also be contributing factors.

    But this only partially explains why the self-styled ‘king of toxic masculinity’ may have based himself here since 2017, and why his poisonous messages had fertile ground in which to germinate.

    Once we understand that, we might be able to start pushing back before it’s too late. 

    Read more

    Why AI-turbocharged misogyny and porn are threats to EU democracy

    Compared to other countries in the region, Romania’s feminist movement is relatively young.

    A fertile ground for toxic masculinity

    In 2000, the Romanian edition of Playboy published a supposedly satirical article titled: “How to Beat Your Wife Without Leaving Marks.”

    The outrage prompted the first major waves of protests and women’s rights activism against gender-based violence and its normalisation in Romanian society.

    But in 2026, Romania ranks low in European rankings on gender equality metrics, and high on incidents of domestic violence.

    Romania has no mandatory gender equality education and no comprehensive sex education, while across swathes of the country, boys and young men lack access to quality education and jobs.

    Successive governments have failed to improve their circumstances, and traditional, social pressure on men to provide for a family or partner fosters anger and resentment.

    The manosphere’s appeal

    This disillusioned generation presents ripe pickings for demagogues like the Tates to sell a cartoonish fantasy of success based on subjugating women. 

    Because of lack of any national data, our organisation helped conduct the first nationally representative study into how rapid social and technological advances are reshaping the values, gender perceptions, and political choices of young Romanian men.

    Our findings show a mixed picture where patriarchal beliefs endure but alongside self-confidence issues over how to bond with women.

    While 53 percent strongly agree that “in a relationship, a woman should be available for sex whenever her partner wants it,” a slightly higher percentage believe that women still do not have adequate rights. 

    The dividing lines are not created by age or urban versus rural but by education and economic precariousness.

    A quarter of respondents with university education agree that a man’s honour must be defended through violence, a figure that rises to 50 percent by those with vocational education.

    Whereas formal education covering these issues is absent, the online environment fills the vacuum and the misogynistic, racist, and homophobic values of the manosphere connect to extreme-right movements in Romania and worldwide.

    Our concerns are that the Tates’ legacy on the minds of young people is so damaging that we may only see the true effects in years to come.

    A better model of masculinity

    But it is never too late to act. In April, Romanian parliament overwhelmingly supported a new law defining the concept of femicide with offenders given potential life sentences.

    The legislation also calls for teaching on gender equality and non-violent relationships to be included in the national curriculum, though this is yet to be implemented.

    Many young men are still open to alternative ideas, so we have time to shape their attitudes and we should not delay – 72 percent interviewed agree democracy is a good form of government but 58 percent want a strong leader who does not bother with parliament or elections. 

    As a riposte to the commercial masculinity bootcamps run by manosphere characters, our organisation runs free and healthy masculinity camps for young men between 18 to 22 years old.

    Led mostly by male trainers, participants from across the country and from a broad socioeconomic background discuss their ideas of masculinity, democracy, extremism, and mental health.

    Many describe loneliness, a lack of physical spaces to build friendships, and a growing guilt for being male.

    Providing young men with a non-judgmental environment to open up is a better way to ensure a safer society, rather than putting the onus on women to change their behaviour. 

    Young men also need to be taught media literacy, so they can recognise hate speech and radicalisation techniques used by the manosphere and the far right to target them.

    Positive male role models can encourage young men to open up about problems, but they also need to be exposed to narratives instilling the values of democracy and pluralism.

    Online platforms remain vastly under-regulated, while offline spaces that provide young people, male and female, with environments in which to socialise and form meaningful connections are lacking. 

    Politicians have successfully harvested the Tates’ audience through skilled social-media targeting, and this bore fruit in the last presidential elections, where young men voted heavily for parties headed by authoritarian leaders.

    The radical right is currently leading the polls, and ongoing political deadlock may yet result in them entering government.

    Young Romanian men are not yet a lost cause, but without a concerted societal effort to combat the sinister forces that influence them, democracy in Romania, and across Europe, may not survive their loss.

      <title>US stock markets and government bonds rally while dollar falls after Democrats secure Congress – business live</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/04/dollar-falls-while-gold-us-treasury-bonds-rally-markets-react-democrats-midterm-election-victory-marks-spencer-latest-live-updates</link>
      <description><p>European shares also power ahead as markets react to blue wave in US midterm elections</p><p>And <strong>Chris Turner</strong>, global head of markets at ING, says:</p><p>Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, <strong>Gina Hinojosa</strong> won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on data centre buildouts.</p><p>Given AI’s role in powering the US economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets. The chip exporter-heavy stock markets of Korea and Taiwan were briefly down 3-4% overnight on news of the blue wave, but have since recouped all those losses.</p><p>For bond investors, the significance of the midterms is ultimately about what they mean for US borrowing. The result makes further significant fiscal expansion harder to deliver through Congress, potentially easing some of the pressure around government borrowing and Treasury issuance.</p><p>That could be supportive for US Treasuries, but it won’t determine the direction of yields on its own. Growth, inflation and the Federal Reserve remain crucial. If the economy slows and inflation continues to ease, there is a stronger case for Treasury yields to move lower.</p><p>Bonds are coming out ​as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the ​chopping block and embrace the higher possibility that further tax ​cuts are put on ice and government spending slows.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/04/dollar-falls-while-gold-us-treasury-bonds-rally-markets-react-democrats-midterm-election-victory-marks-spencer-latest-live-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/china">China</category>

      <description><p>The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history</p><p>Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 04 Nov 2026 15:06:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Irish unemployment remains near historic low of 4.8%]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/irish-unemployment-remains-near-historic-low-of-48/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/irish-unemployment-remains-near-historic-low-of-48/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:52:26 +0000Unemployment in Ireland remained below 5 per cent in October amid reports hiring had strengthened again.

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) said the national rate of joblessness stood at 4.8 per cent last month, up from a revised rate of 4.7 per cent in September.

The seasonally adjusted number of people classified as being unemployed was 143,600 in October, a rise of 5,900 compared with October 2025.

The youth unemployment rate was 11.5 per cent, up from a revised rate of 11.4 per cent in September.

Kate English, chief economist at Deloitte Ireland, said unemployment here has been at 5 per cent or lower since December 2021 (with the exception of 5.1 per cent in March 2026), which she described as “positive”.

“A 5 per cent rate signals resilience and near full employment,” English said.

“The Q3 labour force figures expected in two weeks will be important, as these will capture the number of jobs being added to the economy and the official unemployment rate,” she said.

“Labour market data has delivered a slightly mixed picture with respect to growth in 2026. However, the slowdown in the volume of new jobs being added is clear,” English said.

“While employment growth has softened, there remain clear skills shortages across some parts of the economy, such as in construction,” she said.

Despite the slowdown in employment growth, recruitment company Indeed noted its Irish job postings index had “strengthened”.

“Job postings, a real-time measure of employer demand, stood at 4.1 per cent above their pre-pandemic baseline as of October 23rd of this year compared with 1.9 per cent below baseline at the end of September,” Indeed economist Jack Kennedy said.

“The return of job postings to above their pre-pandemic level is an encouraging indication that employers continue to recruit after hiring demand stabilised earlier this year,” he said.

]]>Devonyu<![CDATA[Oil steadies near one-week highs as US-Iran peace deal hopes dim ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/about-us/advertise/2026/08/11/oil-steadies-near-one-week-highs-as-us-iran-peace-deal-hopes-dim/https://www.irishtimes.com/about-us/advertise/2026/08/11/oil-steadies-near-one-week-highs-as-us-iran-peace-deal-hopes-dim/Tue, 11 Aug 2026 05:01:01 +0000Oil prices steadied on Tuesday at more than ​one-week highs amid fading hopes of a deal between the US and Iran to end their war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, after US president Donald Trump demanded compensation for damage incurred.

Brent crude futures fell 10 cents, or 0.11 per cent, to $87.62 a ​barrel by 0405 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 5 cents, or 0.06 per cent, to $82.08 a barrel. Both benchmarks rose more than ⁠5 per cent on Monday to their highest since July 31st, after Trump responded to Iran’s conditions for ‌a peace ‌deal ​with his own demands that Iran pay compensation for people killed in wars, attacks and protests, which is likely to complicate efforts to reopen the Strait of ⁠Hormuz. Later in the day, he added that ​the US had control of the strait and had swept ​the strategic oil waterway for Iranian mines.

“There appears to be a gulf, no pun intended, between the US and ‌Iran over what any agreement would actually ​look like,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

“As a result, some of the optimism ⁠that built up last week is being unwound, ⁠giving oil prices a ​decidedly bid tone.”

Meanwhile, Saudi Aramco has postponed the restart of its 400,000-barrel-per-day Jazan refinery to August 30th after the Houthis claimed two attacks on the plant on Sunday.

“The chokehold risk around both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb remains highly significant. Even intermittent restrictions or the threat of further incidents keep insurance costs elevated and force longer shipping routes ... hence energy flows look likely to stay constrained near term,” Waterer said.

In a note on Monday, analysts at Barclays said that in ‌the week ending August 7th, ⁠crude oil and refined product net exports through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 3 million barrels per day, down from 4.4 million bpd the previous week.

Markets will likely remain in a state ‌of morbid detachment if oil continues to slip through both blockades via ship-to-ship transfers and overland routes, said IG’s analyst Tony Sycamore. Meanwhile, ​the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) is offering spot crude in a tender, ​its eighth issued since the start of June as the UAE state oil company works to move oil from inside the Strait of Hormuz. - Reuters

]]>Jim Watson<![CDATA[Hydrogen could power Ireland’s expanding data centre sector, Cork conference to hear]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/hydrogen-could-power-irelands-expanding-data-centre-sector-cork-conference-to-hear/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/hydrogen-could-power-irelands-expanding-data-centre-sector-cork-conference-to-hear/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Hydrogen could be used to power Ireland’s expanding data centre sector and ease pressure on the national electricity grid, a conference on hydrogen as a renewable energy will hear later this month.

Prof Rory Monaghan, lead co-ordinator of Sh2amrock, a €54 million EU initiative establishing Ireland’s first hydrogen valley in Galway, said the H2 Summit 2026 in Cork, would see experts explain hydrogen’s huge potential for Ireland and Europe.

“The success of the tech sector in Ireland brings with it the challenge of high electricity demand for data centres. On the supply side, our progress in rolling out wind and solar power means that ever-increasing volumes of clean power are curtailed when power demand is low,” he said.

“Curtailment will increase markedly when offshore wind comes online. Hydrogen, which can be produced from this otherwise wasted electricity and stored, has the potential to provide backup power for large energy users in peak times.”

He explained that hydrogen fuel cells produce electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The hydrogen reacts with oxygen across an electrochemical cell, similar to a battery, to produce electricity, water and small amounts of heat.

Ireland can’t be a dumping ground for data centres other countries don’t want
