]]>SOPA Images<![CDATA[After the SuperValu cyberattack, might your smart fridge be the next target? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:41:50 +0000Do you feel differently about your smart fridge?

The high-tech home hub allows you to check what food you have in, suggest recipes, and manage the family calendar, should you be able to afford its not-insignificant price tag.

But this week’s cyberattack on Supervalu’s refrigeration systems might be forcing people to re-evaluate its position in their home.

Where could the next attack come from?

You might equally be eyeing your connected coffeemaker warily, worried about what it could be getting up behind your back. You might consider unplugging the robot vacuum cleaner in case it goes rogue while you are out on the school run.

Jokes aside, the recent spate of attacks on seemingly harmless systems should give us pause for thought. The problem with many of these connected devices is that as soon as you hook anything up to the internet, it opens up a chink in your armour , no matter how hard we try to lock it down.

It is a trade-off that we might not be aware we are making at the time – but it is a common thread in the modern world. For the sake of convenience, we give up a little security. Even with the most diligent company in charge of maintaining the security of the appliances, there is always a risk that something will go wrong. And with the growth in artificial intelligence (AI), the chance of a previously undetected vulnerability rearing its head has suddenly been magnified.

You might wonder why hackers would want to attack a smart home device in the suburbs of Dublin. While we may not have thousands of euro of stock to destroy, or disposable income to pay out ransoms, we do have something that is valuable: our data. And that, as we know, is worth a lot of money in the right – or wrong – hands.

There is also the chance that our smart home devices, unpatched and open to exploitation, may be used as part of an attack on a high-value target.

In recent days, a joint operation between public and private partners in the tech industry took down a global botnet that had been hidden in set-top boxes across 200 countries. The botnet, which was placed on the devices before they were sold, surreptitiously used the set-top boxes and internet connections of those unlucky enough to have installed them in their homes.

This is not a new threat. Botnets have been carrying out large-scale attacks for years. One example: in 2016, the Mirai botnet took over up to 560,000 unsecured or weak cameras, printers, and DVR players and knocked out Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix, among others.

So what can we do to protect ourselves? Besides cutting off the connection, that is, although you could argue there is no compelling need to have an oven or coffee maker with an internet connection.

There is some help on the way from the bureaucrats, with various rules regarding security being implemented at an EU level, forcing manufacturers to adopt a secure-by-design approach. But we can’t rely on them to fully shield us from all the risks.

There are ways to protect ourselves: keeping up to date with software releases to patch up any security holes is a given;buying reputable brands rather than settling for cheap, unbranded technology from online marketplaces is another. Changing the default passwords on devices is another tip from security experts.

But we need to be aware of what could be coming down the line.

Anthropic recently warned of another threat: that AI models are becoming so smart and small in terms of storage requirements that they could copy themselves into places you might not suspect – such as your smart fridge.

That could create an army of smart botnets that could, in theory, be commanded to launch attacks without needing a data centre to run from. And, the experts argue, that would be one that is very difficult to battle, because there is no centralised point from where the attack has been launched.

Of course it is never as simple as it looks. The scenario proposed by Anthropic was a test rather than a real-world incident, and the end result – a model that replicates itself – is more of a ‘could’ than a ‘did’. The model didn’t have to break in as such, although we are often so lax about security on these connected devices that it wouldn’t have presented a huge barrier if that had been the case.

There are a few lessons to learn here.

Take the prof AI companies about the power and potential of their technology with a grain of salt, for both good and bad.

But perhaps, to be safe, you might also consider limiting smart technology to the essentials. Sometimes the trade-off just isn’t worth it.

Arguably the best tank in the world, the German-made main battle tank was supposed to be a game changer when, after much hand-wringing, it was supplied to Ukraine in 2023 alongside similar behemoths: the British Challenger and the US Abrams. They were predicted to give Ukraine the upper hand over Russia on the battlefield.

They didn’t. What halted the advance of the Russian army and now enforces the stalemate on the battlefield is drones. Lots of them. Cheap and deadly. Made in Ukraine.

History is full of examples of unsuccessful generals who made the mistake of fighting the last war. Instead of adjusting to how the nature of conflict is being changed by technology, they just try to do what worked last time, only better. The Russians, who expected to roll over Ukraine in a couple of weeks based on their previous experience, are just the latest example.

Ireland should be careful not to fall into that trap. The Irish Army obviously needs vehicles but seems to have shaped its future role around turning itself into a conventional armoured brigade that can – don’t say it too loudly – fight alongside other European armies in the sort of battle groups that have been potentially rendered obsolete by the conflict in Ukraine.

The other task that is envisioned for the Army once it’s tooled up is deployment overseas on UN missions. There has not been a UN deployment authorised since 2011, and the mandate for Unifil – Ireland’s most significant deployment in Lebanon – is not being renewed when it runs out at the end of the year.

Not accepting the regrettable but real decline in the global role of the UN is also tantamount to fighting the last war.

The real elephant in the room is where are we going to find the soldiers to fight in these new tanks. The Defence Forces simply does not provide an attractive career for many. That might change. Driving tanks and going overseas are the sort of things that professional soldiers like doing.

Dangers on a train: Russia’s improved drones pose new threat to Ukrainian rail users

But the question that nobody seems to want to ask, however, is whether reshaping the Defence Forces around new armoured vehicles is really the most effective and economical way to defend our land and sea borders now that drones and missiles dominate the battlefield.

Paradoxically, the neglect of the Defence Forces over the years presents Ireland with a unique opportunity to skip a generation of military technology and create a force able to fulfil this goal at a cost that is realistic. And one that could attract the best and brightest engineering and technological talent.

‘Whatever Trump and Putin agree, we’ll fight the invaders’: Inside the dugouts powering Ukraine’s drone war

Our complete lack of a domestic arms industry means that, unlike our larger European partners, we are not trapped by history. Big countries end up locked into feeding their arms manufacturers in what former US president and D-Day commander Dwight Eisenhower dubbed the military-industrial complex.

This includes the French and hence their enthusiasm for selling us tanks. The cost will be enormous. As well as the upfront price, put at about €1 billion, we will be tied into a long-tailed maintenance contract with the French suppliers, which could bring the costs to many multiples of this.

Belgium bought 442 similar vehicles for €1.6 billion, but the lifetime cost is put at €14 billion, or €3.6 million per vehicle. It’s a lot of money for something that could be knocked out by a drone costing a couple of hundred euro.

The potential for marine drones to help police the 880,000sq km of seabed under Ireland’s jurisdiction, including vital submarine cables, is equally obvious for a Naval Service that faces real difficulties crewing its ships.

What adds to the paradox is that we already have a nascent drone industry, but seem determined to stamp it out. The question as to whether Ireland’s security would be better served by investing €14 billion into making our own air and sea drones is one well worth asking before signing a cheque for new tanks.

If the reader’s role was “truly redundant”, this would indicate a “very disorganised” employer, says Michelle Halloran, independent HR consultant and workplace investigator of Halloran HR Resolutions.

“It seems quite odd; it’s a very peculiar decision after only three months that a role is redundant. That sounds very strange to me.

“At best, it doesn’t sound very well organised and doesn’t demonstrate a lot of foresight on the part of the employer,” she says.

While it could have been “sloppy planning”, it might be more justifiable if the company suddenly lost an account or client, and the timing was “just really bad luck” for the reader, she says.

With only three months’ service, the reader was not entitled to any redundancy payment, Halloran says, “so it wasn’t like they were doing her a favour by making the role redundant from a financial perspective”.

Workers require at least two years’ service for statutory entitlements.

]]><![CDATA[Memo to AI: Remember when secretaries were seen as the biggest threat to jobs?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/memo-to-ai-lessons-from-the-rise-and-fall-of-secretarial-skills/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/memo-to-ai-lessons-from-the-rise-and-fall-of-secretarial-skills/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:34:00 +0000At a congress of shorthand writers held in Cincinnati almost 150 years ago, a stenographer called Helen T Pierson took to the stage to rebut male clerks’ growing protests that an influx of women threatened their job security. She took issue, in particular, with the misogynistic argument that women were undercutting men’s salaries because they were willing to work for less pay.

“The injustice of underpaying [women] is so gross and so palpable that it seems an impossibility that such a wrong should continue to exist,” Pierson told the mainly male audience. “It is hard and unfair in the extreme that a woman should be underpaid simply because she is a woman, and is not only unfair, but is calculated to do much harm.”

As with software and AI today, the mass adoption of shorthand and typing changed work habits and roles. But not all workers benefited. As new technology sweeps away the last vestiges of these older office productivity tools, what can we learn about how they were applied and misapplied?

First, try not to be too optimistic.

By the 1880s, supercharged by the rapid spread of office work, the typewriter and shorthand – the 2,000-year-old technique of using written symbols to speed the recording and transcription of speech – had combined to create new job opportunities for many women.

Before office work expanded in the US and Europe, social norms confined most of them to traditional “female roles” such as teaching or domestic service. But shorthand and especially typing were marketed as particularly suited to the female mentality and physique. By 1900, three-quarters of shorthand typists in the US were women – hence the distress of male clerks. Their protests were in vain. By 1930, 95 per cent of the US profession were women.

Yet shorthand and typing were a double-edged sword. Given a chance to enter the workforce, some women thrived. For instance, many British suffragists and suffragettes were expert typists who used their office skills as levers of emancipation, for instance, to prepare, print and distribute leaflets.

Secretarial skills also helped the first women stockbrokers, journalists and publishers break into their professions. Others enjoyed secretarial work simply for the flexibility and cash it provided to develop other career paths.

But many shorthand typists were consigned to life under a very low glass ceiling, far removed from the rosy imaginings of the late 19th century’s women pioneers. The determination and sacrifices required to progress in full-time paid work were sometimes too great.

The second lesson is that the intervention of aggressive consultants, selling technology on grounds of efficiency, is often bad for the people at the sharp end of that implementation.

By the 1910s, “scientific managers”, inspired by consultant Frederick Winslow Taylor’s mechanistic push to make manufacturing more efficient, were putting speedometers on typewriters to assess productivity. One Taylor disciple, William Henry Leffingwell, author of 1917’s Scientific Office Management, obsessed over the best way secretaries should arrange a desk (“keeping stationery in desk drawers is [a] source of waste motion”), how long it should take to insert a sheet of paper in a typewriter (three one-hundredths of a minute), and whether it paid to take paper clips off correspondence before filing (it depends: it takes 10 minutes to remove one pound of clips, he calculated).

Leffingwell was naturally a big advocate of the typing pool, which grouped shorthand typists together rather than relying on “small groups of uncontrolled stenographers throughout the office who work only part of their time on letters and part on miscellaneous clerical tasks and, as is often the case, sit in absolute idleness at other times”.

Historian Lucienne Boyce, who worked as a temporary secretary in the 1970s, says: “The whole image of the typing pool was of a factory, and the women became instruments ... just as you keep workers down in a factory, by giving them a tiny bit of job to do.” Boyce later became a careers adviser and saw how rarely men were directed down the secretarial path.

This was a world where “bosses, almost always male, literally dictate to female clericals”, as academic Catherine Rankovic has put it. As the century progressed, the combination of complete control, a rigid focus on efficiency, and lower status sucked from the office what little autonomy and joy women had hoped they might achieve there. It created what sociologist Margery Davies called a “secretarial proletariat”.

Obstacles that stood in the way of these women included formal or informal marriage bars, inadequate or non-existent maternity leave or childcare options, and looming disparities between the pay and promotion opportunities offered to women, not to mention casual sexism and outright sexual harassment.

A third lesson is that the same forces that lead to the birth of one technology can also hasten its demise at the hands of the next wave of development. The earlier technology’s users are often the unwitting victims. The Dictaphone, the electric typewriter, the computer and the internet finally put paid to the typing pool and consigned shorthand dictation to the shredder of secretarial skills.

With the advent of the desktop personal computer, the typewriter became a “keyboard” and the association of typing with women’s work broke down. Executives started to realise the quickest route from the idea in their heads to the memo or letter was through their own fingertips. “Now computers have come along, and ‘typing’ is ‘keyboarding’. Suddenly, voila! Men can type,” Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist, said in a 2007 commencement address at her alma mater Smith College. “Gives you faith in men’s ability to change, doesn’t it?”

So the dream that many women nursed in the late 19th century – that innovations such as shorthand and typing would provide a route into the workplace and a launch platform for promotion – was, for many, a hollow one. Only in the 2020s did women managers start to outnumber secretaries in the list of most common roles for women in the US.

But there is a fourth, and more upbeat, lesson from the rise and fall of the secretarial proletariat. New technologies can create opportunities for a smaller number of workers to cultivate skills that enable them to shape better jobs for themselves.

Secretaries have morphed into high-value personal and executive assistants, for instance, increasingly sought after for their command of the newest office tools.

Rebecca Siciliano, managing director of agency Tiger Recruitment, says a lot of her clients “want someone [who] is AI and tech savvy”.

These assistants must provide the expert human touch needed to juggle diaries packed with virtual and in-person meetings, and to represent their boss inside and outside the business. They need to know when to delegate to bots the more mundane tasks of taking minutes or updating spreadsheets. The best command salaries of £85,000 annually, according to Siciliano. Some may rise to become chiefs of staff and operations managers.

Much has changed since Pierson made the case for women in the workplace. The manual typewriter is long gone in most offices. The smartphone and AI are eradicating the last remnants of need for written shorthand. And despite Tiger and its clients’ best efforts to broaden the pool of executive assistants, only a small minority are men.

“I see on the ground that students are using AI tools to develop CVs, based on the job interview. They’re asking AI to produce an actual CV based on the job application, and they’re firing that in. Rather than completing generic CVs based on job descriptions, she recommends that graduates build off these templates, and consider how their skills match the role they’re applying for. She also reminds graduates to avoid typing all of their personal details into AI.

She says most recruiters can tell quite easily if a CV has been fully generated by AI. “You can see the poor formatting on them, and the language is so Americanised. So people know if they’re written by AI.”

Employers increasingly concerned about job candidates using AI to write CVs

Another place where she sees graduates fall down is applying to too many roles with these AI-generated CVs. “They’re firing off these CVs to everybody and anybody for selection,” she says. Graduates need to ask themselves “what kind of company do you want to work in?”

Curran recommends writing down all the companies you’re applying for in a journal, and reflecting on whether these are places you really want to work.

Graduates should have a “story bank” prepared for applications and interviews, which allows them to not only identify the relevant skills and expertise they have, but demonstrate where they picked up this experience.

Today’s graduates should have “emotional intelligence, critical thinking, all the things that a human person can only do”, she says. For graduates considering applying for jobs outside of Ireland, she says AI can be a “great research tool”.

I can pull up all the information around European job listings. I can look into different companies on a European level. The likes of the EU are recruiting huge amounts of graduates at the moment.”

Graduate job coaches offering access to the ‘unwritten rules’ of recruitment

Another way graduates can utilise AI on their side is to use it to practise for job interviews. Curran says applicants can use tools that allow them to practice talking with an AI chat bot ahead of their interview. Listening back to yourself will allow you to improve “how you present yourself and, better your communication skills”, she says.

Finally, Curran reminds graduates that while it may feel like there’s only one way to complete job applications in an era of AI, traditional methods have not gone away.

Using online networks such as LinkedIn to see if you know someone working in a company, or chatting to friends and family members to see if their workplaces have openings is another way graduates can get a foot in the door.

“Start at smaller employers, local employers. Walk with your feet, print your CV out. I’ve seen graduates being really successful with that.”

]]><![CDATA[How can my son find out if his father has cut him out of his will?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000My son’s father and I never married. He has never paid maintenance for him. A few years ago there was a disagreement between them and unfortunately his father hasn’t had any contact with him for about five years.

My ex also has another son who he is very close to. Recently my ex came into some money from the sale of his own father’s house. In the event that he dies, how can our son find out if he left a will?

CC

In an ideal world, we all take care of family, not least when we die, assuming we have the resources to do so. The real world is more messy.

You don’t say whether your former partner was ever a part of your son’s life but he certainly never paid anything to the cost of raising him.

Now middle-aged, your son and his father no longer talk. Meanwhile, his father has a son from a separate relationship to whom he is close, and the father has come into money.

That certainly raises the potential for a dispute when he dies.

There are two scenarios here – one where he has a will and one where he does not. Let’s take them in reverse order.

If there is no will, his estate would be divided according to the Succession Act.

You do not say whether the father ever married – either to the mother of his other son or someone else. If he did, and presuming that spouse survives him, she will receive two-thirds of his estate with his children sharing the final third.

That would include your son, this favoured other son and any other children he might have.

If the spouse does not survive him, or there never was any spouse, the children split the value of the estate between them without regard to favourites. Everything is split evenly.

Whomever applies for the grant of administration intestate is obliged to track down all qualifying beneficiaries – which includes all children regardless of whether they were born inside or outside a marriage. In practice, whomever applies to manage the estate will engage a solicitor as intestacy can be a minefield.

But what if there is a will?

If it is like most other Irish wills and there is a spouse, it will simply leave everything to the spouse. If he does not, the spouse is entitled to what is called a legal right share – which, where there are children, amounts to one-third of the estate.

Assuming any legal right share is respected, the will could make provision for one or other or both sons – and any other children – but it doesn’t have to. There is no obligation for a person to provide in death for adult children or any other relative apart from a spouse.

However, if a child feels that they should be entitled to something in a will, they can take what is called a section 117 action.

Section 117 (1) of the Succession Act 1965 says: “Where, on application by or on behalf of a child of a testator, the court is of opinion that the testator has failed in his moral duty to make proper provision for the child in accordance with his means, whether by his will or otherwise, the court may order that such provision shall be made for the child out of the estate as the court thinks just.”

This is a very wide and nebulous position, with the court taking into account the circumstances of the applicant vis-à-vis other family members among other things.

It clarifies in section 117 (2): “The court shall consider the application from the point of view of a prudent and just parent, taking into account the position of each of the children of the testator and any other circumstances which the court may consider of assistance in arriving at a decision that will be as fair as possible to the child to whom the application relates and to the other children.”

The key thing is that any section 117 application must be made to the court within six months of a grant of probate.

And how do you know probate has been granted? In a harmonious family situation, you’d expect to be notified of this but in the scenario you outline, it may be a case of your son keeping tabs on the Probate Register where all grants of probate and grants on administration (in case of intestacy) are recorded – along with copies of the related will where one exists.

He will need his father’s first and surname and the year in which he died.

When will probate be granted? That depends on how efficiently whoever is managing the estate sort the paperwork and how complex the estate is. It generally takes a year or close to it anyway.

Is it worth pursuing a section 117? That depends on your son’s position in life and also what his father’s estate comprises. There is certainly no guarantee of success and there will be legal fees to consider.

Of course, there is nothing to say that this money your ex has recently come into will still be part of his estate when he dies. It could well have been dissipated by then – either because it was spent or because it was gifted to other family members.

The Section 117 procedure only refers to provision in a will or lack thereof. It does not cover lifetime gifts.

]]>Robert Kirk<![CDATA[Opinion polls are core to how media covers politics, but is that a good thing?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/03/opinion-polls-are-core-to-how-media-covers-politics-but-is-that-a-good-thing/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/03/opinion-polls-are-core-to-how-media-covers-politics-but-is-that-a-good-thing/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000On Tuesday, Americans vote in midterm elections with consequences for everyone around the world. As usual, much of the campaign coverage has revolved around opinion polls, which give the Democrats a national lead of up to 11 points on the generic congressional ballot, while the party’s candidates are challenging for Senate seats in places where they usually wouldn’t have a hope.

Despite all that polling data, many remain sceptical about whether these predictions will be proved correct. Regardless, polls have been central to the coverage, as they are in most elections.

Polling has been a fixture of political journalism for almost 90 years. Its modern form dates from 1936, when George Gallup used a small but carefully chosen sample to predict Franklin Roosevelt’s landslide, humiliating the Literary Digest, whose vast survey of its own affluent readers had backed his opponent. Gallup’s results were syndicated to newspapers across the country, beginning a partnership between pollsters and the press that has lasted ever since.

But it was not until the 1970s, or in Ireland’s case the 1980s, that newspapers began to invest seriously in polls of their own. The Market Research Bureau of Ireland, founded by Jack Jones in 1962, spent years researching washing powder and air travel before turning to politics, and the Irish Times/MRBI series that began in the early 1980s became the benchmark here.

There has been no shortage of criticism of the relationship. Newspapers, it is suggested, over-dramatise results, splashing shouty headlines about tiny shifts that are within the margin of error. Polling is also blamed for “horse race” coverage that treats elections as sporting fixtures, ignoring the issues at stake. One Harvard study of the 2016 US presidential race found policy accounted for just a tenth of coverage, less than a quarter of the space devoted to who was ahead.

These criticisms are not without foundation, although research across 27 European countries suggests poll-driven coverage is most common in tight, multiparty contests, where knowing the state of play can help voters decide how to use their ballots.

Distrust of the polls themselves has also grown, with people pointing to glaring misses such as Brexit or Donald Trump’s first victory. That has been compounded by the rise of populist movements whose supporters are often underrepresented in surveys, prompting accusations of bias. Despite all this, a study of more than 200 elections in 32 countries found no evidence that polling errors were increasing.

Three elections in the past 10 days have highlighted some of these issues. In Brazil, the final surveys had incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead in the first round, which his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro edged, then gave Bolsonaro a narrow lead in the runoff, which Lula won by more than three points. Neither error was particularly large, but each picked the wrong winner.

In Israel, the final polls correctly predicted deadlock but underestimated both Likud and the Arab parties.

And in Serbia, where public polling is sparse and voters had reason to be wary of declaring opposition sympathies, surveys showing Aleksandar Vucic’s party narrowly ahead were proved completely wrong when the student-led opposition won an outright majority.

The Irish Times view on Serbia’s election: youthquake in Belgrade

Traditional polling is being reshaped by changes in the media industry. Falling revenues have made publishers less enthusiastic about the expensive business of high-quality polling. That has led to a move from face-to-face interviewing towards cheaper online panels, weighted to reflect the profile of the electorate.

In Ireland, Red C for the Business Post and Ireland Thinks for the Sunday Independent now alternate monthly online surveys, while The Irish Times’s face-to-face poll with Ipsos B&A appears several times a year. The methods can return somewhat different results. Red C, for example, regularly puts Fianna Fáil a few points lower than other pollsters do. But overall performance has been respectable, with final polls in 2024 largely within the margin of error. Every poll is a snapshot in time, and across volatile referendum campaigns, surveys and results have often diverged wildly.

The field has narrowed too, with titles such as the Sunday Times Irish edition no longer commissioning polls.

Elsewhere, there are signs of questionable standards. In September, an undercover investigation by Channel 4 News and the Verbatim group revealed that polls carried prominently by the Times and the Telegraph had been arranged by Reform UK figures and paid for through what they believed was an American donor’s company, without either paper being told.

In the US, a firm called Wedgewood Polls admitted last week that it had fabricated results reported by The New York Times, Newsweek and others. One Michigan Democratic candidate says a fake survey showing her in single digits drove away her donors and ended her Senate campaign.

The problem in both cases lay with news organisations failing to verify where the numbers came from and what financial incentives might have been involved. But what is even worse is that some US outlets are giving prominence to the almost completely unregulated prediction markets that have mushroomed in recent years. CNN and CNBC have partnerships with Kalshi, and Wall Street Journal owner Dow Jones with Polymarket, on undisclosed terms.

This seems a highly dubious proposition, since betting odds can be moved by anyone with deep enough pockets. The old model, in which media organisations paid for polls and stood over the results, may have had its flaws but this particular replacement looks considerably worse.

]]><![CDATA[Don’t make an additional voluntary contribution to your pension – until you read this]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000Retirement savers have just another two weeks or so until the November 18th deadline for tax relief on additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) for 2025 passes.

Often described as “turbo fuel” for your pension, the benefits of these payments are many. You can maximise available tax relief, improve your chances of retiring early, and you’ll hopefully have a bigger fund to draw down in retirement thanks to them.

But before you lock your money away through AVCs, it’s also worth taking a moment to consider if they are the best option for your money at a particular point in time.

Your money is locked away

Once you put additional money into your pension, it is locked away until you can retire. But what if you need it for your health? Your children? To pay down expensive debts? Repairs on your house, or just for those holidays you want to take now, rather than wait until retirement?

“It’s really a case of having a financial plan – and prioritising what’s most important,” says Mark Ryan, director of My Wealth Management.

Putting money into the stock market, an investment fund, or a high-yielding deposit account can still give you the potential for real gains, while maintaining flexibility. Of course, you are giving up on the tax relief – but this might be okay.

“Tax relief, while it’s great, shouldn’t be the only consideration. It’s of little benefit if it leaves you short of money for other needs,” says Sinead McEvoy, head of retirement solutions at Standard Life.

For McEvoy, a solid approach can be doing “a bit of both”. Put some money into a rainy-day fund, for example, and some into an AVC.

She is often asked whether or not you should prioritise your pension, or paying your mortgage.

Managing your money and your time in retirement

For some, the psychological impact of paying off a mortgage is huge, and this can take priority when it comes to spare cash. But focusing on it solely may not be the right approach either.

“I don’t think I’d pay off all your mortgage and ignore your pension,” she says. “Think of all the compounding you’re missing out on by paying off your mortgage.”

“It would be a preference for some people,” Ryan agrees, referring to paying down the mortgage first. Another option, he suggests, is to boost your AVCs now, and hope for investment growth, and use the bigger lump sum when you retire to pay down the mortgage at that point.

You won’t benefit from the same tax relief as AVCs by paying down your mortgage, so it can be worthwhile to “crunch the numbers” before making a decision.

Indeed, there can be an opportunity cost of this approach; you are giving up on tax relief, which can supercharge your pension fund.

Consider €200 invested every month for 10 years. If it returns an average of 6 per cent a year, it will deliver almost €32,500. But if tax relief had been available, at the higher rate, you would have had €280 going into the investment each month – so the return would have been significantly higher, at €45,500. You just wouldn’t have been able to withdraw it.

You may end up paying a higher tax rate in retirement

“I get asked this question often,” says Ryan. “Why would I put in money to get tax relief at 40 per cent when I pay it at the same rate in retirement?”

Remember, the tax relief you enjoy on AVCs is only deferred; when you draw down your pension, you may pay income tax on it. So then, you need to bear in mind the value of this tax relief – while it will grow tax-free, which is very beneficial, it can be particularly valuable if you get relief on it today as a higher rate taxpayer, and draw it down at the standard rate of tax in retirement.

While a higher tax rate in retirement is indicative of a healthy fund, it may be a consideration for those close to the higher tax bracket.

“Those on the borderline (of the higher rate), and considering AVCs, then it’s a conversation worth having,” says Ryan. “I have had scenarios where people have decided not to do AVCs because of that.”

Others, however, will opt for the ‘bird in the hand’ approach, and take what’s on offer now – tax relief – rather than predict how the future might play out.

This decision may be only for a certain cohort, however. First of all, to maximise your tax-free lump sum on retirement of €200,000, you will need a fund of €800,000 – 25 per cent is tax-free; amounts between €200,000 and €500,000 are taxed at 20 per cent. “And that’s a significant pension fund for most,” says McEvoy. “Typically, people are underfunding their pensions.”

Lessons for a happy retirement from a year interviewing Ireland’s top leaders

So, paying in AVCs can help bump up your tax-free lump sum.

And, paying tax at the higher rate on your pension “just isn’t the case for most people” says McEvoy, pointing to the more generous tax bands available for the over-65s.

As our table shows, a married couple with an annual pension income of €36,126 won’t pay any tax in retirement, while single people aged 65 and over won’t pay tax on earnings of less than €18,000.

However, as income rises, retirees will see a growing proportion of their income taxed at the higher rate. A single person earning €45,563 from a combination of state pension and private pension income, for example, will pay a certain portion of their income at the higher rate of 40 per cent (€1,563 for 2026), thus pushing their effective rate up to 12.3 per cent. And it increases from there; someone earning €75,563 a year in retirement will pay the top rate of tax on €31, 563 of their income – for an effective tax rate of 24.5 per cent.

AVCs have to be drawn down at the same time as an occupational pension

Having different pension vehicles in play may give you greater flexibility as to when you have to draw down your pension. PRSAs (Personal Retirement Savings Accounts), for example, can be drawn down between 60 – or 50 if it isn’t tied to an employment – and 75. It might also help keep your pension income in retirement taxed at the lower rate.

Remember, however AVCs are funded – either through the main scheme or an AVC PRSA – they are tied to this main scheme.

“When you have an AVC, it must be retired at the same time as the main scheme,” says McEvoy. So, there is no flexibility available when putting your AVC money into a separate pension vehicle.

However, there might be the opportunity to segment your pension into different PRSAs at retirement, so that you can draw them down at different ages.

There is some flexibility, however, if you’re not happy with the fund choices offered in your occupational/public sector scheme.

AVC PRSAs can be used to offer greater investment choice. But the charges might be higher than in your occupational scheme, so this should be considered.

What are AVCs?

In short, AVCs are additional payments you make to your occupational or public sector pension to boost your fund, and hopefully your income in retirement.

If you have already maximised your matching contributions (ie, your employer contributes 6 per cent of salary if you contribute 6 per cent), and you have extra cash, you can consider putting this into your pension via an AVC.

As with all pension savings, the big advantage here is the tax relief you get – if you’re a higher rate taxpayer, for example, a €1,000 contribution to your pension will only cost you €600.

How much you can contribute and avail of tax relief will depend on Revenue limits. Tax relief is offered as a percentage of your net earnings, and increases in line with your age. So, if you’re aged between 30 and 39, for example, you can put 20 per cent of your earnings into your pension and get tax relief on it (so up to €10,000 a year if you earn €50,000, for example). This percentage increases to 30 per cent for those aged 50-54; 35 per cent for 55-59; and 40 per cent for 60 and over.

When it comes to making an AVC, you can do so on a regular or one-off basis, so they offer good flexibility. A maximum annual limit of €115,000 applies.

If you haven’t made AVCs for 2025, and you do so before the online tax return deadline of November 18th, you will be due a tax saving.

The charges and fees are mandated at EU level, with delivery companies given the legal responsibility to collect them if the levies have not been paid during online checkout.

The new charge is intended to cover the increased costs incurred by customs authorities due to the huge growth of ecommerce in recent years. It will apply to all goods, regardless of their value, once a seller ships them to Ireland from outside the EU.

The growth in online marketplaces – based in China primarily – has caused dramatic upheaval in retail. According to official estimates, about six billion packages with a value of less than €150 came into EU states from outside the bloc last year.

The EU handling fee of €2 per item adds a further €6 to the bill, bringing the total end cost to €25.

Consumers will be expected to pay the charges in one of two ways.

Some larger ecommerce operations will be set up to collect the customs duty and EU handling fee at the point of sale.

In such circumstances, both charges will be shown to the consumer and the total price paid at the checkout will be the final price, with no extra charges on delivery.

Other websites may not collect these charges at checkout and the delivery company will be required to collect the money from the consumer.

When charges have to be collected in this way it is likely a further administrative fee of about €7 will be added to the total by the delivery company.

In such cases, the three small items that had an initial price tag totalling €10 could end up costing Irish consumers €32, or more than three times the original value.

There is no customs duty or EU handling fee if goods are based in Ireland, Northern Ireland or in another EU member state at the time they are ordered.

As we have seen though, it can leave them vulnerable, too. One security issue was enough to cause millions of euro worth of damage across several countries.

Regardless of the motivation, we should take this incident as a warning. The next attack may not be so easily dealt with, nor its impact as short-lived.

]]><![CDATA[Makhlouf says Philip Lane would be ‘great’ candidate to succeed Lagarde]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/makhlouf-says-philip-lane-would-be-great-candidate-to-succeed-lagarde/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/makhlouf-says-philip-lane-would-be-great-candidate-to-succeed-lagarde/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 12:59:43 +0000Central Bank of Ireland governor Gabriel Makhlouf said he believes European Central Bank (ECB) chief economist Philip Lane would be a “great” candidate to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the ECB.

“I think Philip would be great but I don’t know whether legally doing a further term on the executive board is possible,” he said.

Lane’s term as chief economist expires in May.

“Ireland should support the best candidate,” Makhlouf told reporters at a finance conference in Croke Park on Monday.

Lagarde announced last week she intended to leave her post next February, nine months before her term ends, triggering a succession race with former Dutch and Spanish central bank governors Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos seen as the front-runners.

Lagarde’s decision to step down early came as ECB policymakers held interest rates steady despite the pickup in headline inflation from higher energy prices.

Makhlouf said he “seriously considered” supporting a rate hike but decided based on the evidence “holding was the right thing”.

“I made that decision for last week based on what I saw in the numbers last week,” he said.

“We live in very, very uncertain times, exceptionally uncertain times, and we have got to keep a very close eye on the evidence in the data.”

Key candidates to replace ECB president Christine Lagarde

With markets predicting another quarter-point ECB rate increase in December, Makhlouf reiterated the bank’s mantra that decisions would be made on a meeting-by-meeting basis, based on the data.

The impact of US midterm elections on global financial stability was difficult to predict, he said, and would depend on the outcome of the elections.

In his address to the conference, Makhlouf warned an equity price correction relating to supercharged AI valuations would not be a “surprise”.

“The US is where the market correction would start,” he said. “The important thing for us is to really understand the transmission channels that would transmit whatever shock happened in the US.”

Makhlouf also said the Government should be saving more of Ireland’s corporate tax windfall in its two wealth funds. “Putting more into them would be a good thing,” he said.

“What the funds have been set up for are the cost of transitions that are definitely coming; they are not speculative. Demographic change and climate change are definitely going to impact the economy.”

Why are interest rates so high – and how exposed is Ireland?

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council has warned the Government is planning to spend up to 90 per cent of expected receipts from corporate tax over the next five years.

Makhlouf said using this revenue to support current spending was risky given the concentration risk.

About half of last year’s €33 billion corporate tax haul came from just three companies.

]]>Eamonn Farrell<![CDATA[O’Leary commits to Ryanair expansion in Dublin next year but says air fares will rise]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/ryanair-weighs-cost-cuts-to-counter-high-fuel-bills/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/ryanair-weighs-cost-cuts-to-counter-high-fuel-bills/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 07:04:46 +0000Ireland’s biggest airport could grow strongly next year but travellers will pay higher air fares, Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary predicted on Monday.

High fuel bills left Ryanair’s profits for the six months to September 30th trailing the same period last year by 15 per cent at €2.15 billion, the airline reported.

Speaking after the Dublin-based carrier published financial results, O’Leary cautioned that air fares would rise in Europe next year as airlines grappled with increased fuel costs sparked by the US-Iran war.

Ryanair would need a 20 per cent increase in ticket prices to cover a fuel bill that the airline says could be €2 billion higher.

“But I don’t think the market will bear that,” O’Leary said. He calculated that prices could still rise by more than 10 per cent.

O’Leary repeated a pledge to add aircraft and two million seats at Dublin Airport in 2027 if the Irish Aviation Authority goes through with a proposal to cut charges levied on airlines there.

“We think Dublin could grow very strongly next year,” O’Leary said.

The airport could handle up to 40 million passengers by 2028, up from more than 37.5 million this year, he predicted.

Celebrated Sri Lankan cricketer claims Ryanair staff at Dublin Airport were ‘discriminatory’

That would bring numbers into line with a proposed increase in the airport’s controversial passenger cap, which Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien is expected to approve in coming months.

Next year’s likely growth highlights the need to axe the Dublin passenger cap altogether, O’Leary said.

“There are two runways so it can do 60 million, that’s the only cap that should be applied,” he said.

Ryanair plans to cut costs next year to counter rising fuel bills.

That could include freezing pay after April 2027 for unions that have not agreed increases before then.

Irish, British, Spanish and Portuguese unions have yet to strike pay deals with the carrier, but most others across Europe have done so, according to O’Leary.

Other measures will include using artificial intelligence to boost productivity in support and back office, and slowing the rate at which it hires new crews.

Ryanair to close bag drop earlier in effort to give passengers time to clear security

Ryanair bought 80 per cent of its fuel needs for the 12 months to March 2027 at $67 (€60) a barrel in advance.

But a doubling in the cost of the remaining fuel contributed to a 10 per cent increase in costs over the six months to September 30th.

The airline has hedged 25 per cent of what it needs for its next financial year at $99 a barrel, O’Leary confirmed.

Revenue rose 3 per cent to €10.8 billion during the six-month period, the first half of Ryanair’s financial year, but average fares dipped 4 per cent to €57.50, the airline said on Monday.

Ryanair flew almost 126 million passengers during the six months, an increase of 6 per cent.

It has cut predicted passenger numbers for the 12 months to March 31st to 214 million from 215 million, O’Leary said.

He cautioned that profit for the current financial year remains “highly sensitive to adverse external developments”, including wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, fuel prices and European air traffic control disruption.

Farewell to ‘aeroplane mode’: Flying loses its status as the last internet black hole

Ryanair will pay an interim dividend of 27.3 cent a share.

It also pledged to buy back €800 million worth of shares over 10 months from February.

The airline had €2.6 billion cash at the end of September. Its shares were up 3.5 per cent at €23.71 in Dublin shortly after 1pm on Monday.

]]>Olivier Hoslet

Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

The outcome received a positive reaction from Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally.

🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen?

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing.

Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT

— NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026

Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.”

“As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.”

Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration.

It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland.

 

Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”.

“We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński.

“If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added.

.@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l

— Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026

The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump.

Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it.

“Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority.

Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”.

Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026

Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki.

Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results, while his senior aides have also said little on the outcome. One exception was Marcin Przydacz, the head of Nawrocki’s International Policy Bureau.

“As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.”

Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections.

Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje…

— Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026

Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans agead of the midterms.

Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”.

On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.”

pic.twitter.com/r6h2B5WfWa

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) November 4, 2026

]]> International Commission of Jurists criticises takeover of Polish constitutional court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/04/international-commission-of-jurists-criticises-takeover-of-polish-constitutional-court/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:05:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106374

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”.

However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis around the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament.

🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings.

🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx

— ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026

On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties.

Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence.

Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS, has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”.

The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton.

In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate.

 

“At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.”

In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”.

Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański.

The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government.

Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026

The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO.

On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal.

It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”.

Pełna treść stanowiska: https://t.co/OvJPpaGDel pic.twitter.com/2UpV2itgcd

— Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) October 31, 2026

That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska.

Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”.

Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored.

However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”

]]> Disputed Polish constitutional court holds first meeting after takeover by government-backed judges https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/03/disputed-polish-constitutional-court-holds-first-meeting-after-takeover-by-government-backed-judges/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:33:46 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106353

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski.

However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”.

Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend.

PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026

The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control.

Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska.

For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present.

However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed.

 

The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges.

None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached.

They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges.

That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached.

Zgromadzenie Ogólne TK: JEST KWORUM! 👏
Według przedstawionej interpretacji liczy się je od 12 uprawnionych osób. 2/3 × 12 = 8.
Prawo i matematyka.👏 pic.twitter.com/77v2ep9HbT

— Pani Prezes 👠 (@PaniNaSzpilkach) November 3, 2026

Once that issue was agreed, the eight judges present proceeded to decide upon a number of key issues. First, they adopted a draft budget for the TK for 2027, something that Święczkowski had been unable to achieve, which was used as an argument for his ousting.

Second, they drew lots to decide which of the TK’s judges would sit on disciplinary panels for Święczkowski and Sochański in relation to their suspension from the court.

However, some legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether a legal quorum was established at today’s meeting. Ryszard Piotrowski, a prominent constitutional scholar, called the meeting “illegal”, reports news website Onet. Przemysław Rosati, the president of the Supreme Bar Council, also expressed his doubts.

Obniżenie progu kworum na skutek zawieszenia prezesa i wiceprezesa otwiera puszkę Pandory. To jest mechanizm, który pozwala dowolnie obniżać kworum na Zgromadzeniu Ogólnym TK – wystarczy, że prezes zawiesi 10 sędziów i będzie mógł na Zgromadzeniu podejmować decyzję w trzy osoby.…

— Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) November 3, 2026

Święczkowski himself rejected the legitimacy of what he called a “social gathering”, saying that Korwin-Piotrowska is a “usurper” who has no right to call a general assembly at all, reported Polsat News.

Shortly before the meeting at the TK, Nawrocki also met with the prime minister, Donald Tusk, for the first time since the crisis at the court broke out last Friday. They had convened at the presidential palace for a meeting of the National Security Council that Nawrocki had called before the TK crisis.

During public remarks broadcast before the confidential meeting got underway, Nawrocki accused the government of “illegally taking over the Constitutional Tribunal”. He added that Tusk “bears full responsibility for…all these illegal actions”.

Grubo! Karol Nawrocki do Tuska:

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal.

Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence.

At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker.

The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon.

Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners.

Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years.

Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”.

 

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.

It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund.
