The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found.

In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025

An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained.

Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law.

“I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”.

 

Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge.

In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled.

Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed.

Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:01:18 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Sequoia scraps London office as UK employees face axe https://www.cityam.com/sequoia-scraps-london-office-as-uk-employees-face-axe/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:24:17 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474492

Silicon Valley venture capital giant Sequoia Capital is shutting its London office and cutting staff, just six years after expanding into Europe, in a major retreat from Britain’s startup investment scene. The US investor, an early backer of Apple, Airbnb and Stripe, confirmed the closure in a sweeping restructuring announcement, saying it no longer saw [...]]]>

Silicon Valley venture capital giant Sequoia Capital is shutting its London office and cutting staff, just six years after expanding into Europe, in a major retreat from Britain’s startup investment scene.

The US investor, an early backer of Apple, Airbnb and Stripe, confirmed the closure in a sweeping restructuring announcement, saying it no longer saw the need for a physical presence in the capital.

“We are closing our London office, which means several people will be leaving Sequoia”, the firm said in a blog post published on Wednesday.

“This is not about the team – they are excellent. We simply don’t see the need for a local presence”.

Sequoia insisted it remained committed to backing European startups but said investment decisions and support would increasingly be handled from its Silicon Valley headquarters.

“We believe that Europe will continue to produce outlier founders and companies, and that we can continue to provide world class support from our home base in the Bay Area”.

The decision reverses Sequoia’s European expansion, which began in 2020 when it opened its London office and hired former Accel investor Luciana Lixandru to lead its regional operations.

By 2023, the firm had expanded its London investment team to six partners.

London loses Silicon Valley heavyweight

The withdrawal comes despite London’s recovery as Europe’s leading technology investment hub.

UK startups raised $23.7bn (£17.8bn) in venture capital last year, up 33 per cent on 2024, according to Dealroom figures commissioned by the government.

London accounted for almost three-quarters of that investment, while the capital reclaimed its position ahead of Paris in global technology ecosystem rankings earlier this year.

However, Britain’s startup sector remains heavily dependent on overseas investors, with foreign capital accounting for 74 per cent of UK venture funding in 2025.

Sequoia’s exit comes as the government attempts to encourage more investment into British startups, including through tax incentives announced in last week’s Budget.

The closure forms part of a broader shake-up at the venture capital heavyweight, which has also scrapped its Arc accelerator and Scouts programmes, streamlined investment teams and removed the distinction between early-stage and growth investing.

The firm said it was moving towards a more selective investment strategy, concentrating resources on fewer companies.

“We are best at high-conviction, highly selective venture capital investing. This is our focus”, it said.

The restructuring follows a leadership transition and comes despite Sequoia raising approximately $10bn in new funds, underlining that its London withdrawal is a strategic decision rather than an apparent shortage of investment capital.

The firm said its priority was delivering stronger returns rather than expanding its global footprint. “Our objective function is not scale, but quality”, it added.

Workwear brand Strauss has warned it will relinquish sponsor rights for next year’s Ice Hockey World Championships if Russia is allowed to participate.

The Germany company says it will scrap all branding at the competition and would consider withdrawing its support altogether if the International Ice Hockey Federation lifts a ban on Russia in place since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

It puts the IHHF in a difficult position following the Russian Ice Hockey Federation’s successful appeal against the ban at the Court of Arbitration for Sport last week.

“We have been a partner of the Ice Hockey World Championship for many years and value our collaboration with the IIHF,” said Strauss CEO Henning Strauss. 

“Should Russia’s national team participate in the 2027 World Championship in Germany as a result of the CAS ruling, we will forgo all logo exposure associated with the tournament. We are also considering withdrawing as a sponsor.”

Strauss is also a sponsor of European football’s governing body, Uefa, and this season expanded its deal to become refereeing partner – a move that sees its logo appear on officials’ sleeves in the men’s and women’s Champions League.

Why Russia may be allowed back in ice hockey

The Cas ruling ordered the IIHF to allow Russia to compete at both the men’s and women’s World Championships and equivalent junior events that precede them.

Cas said its three-man panel “found that the IIHF arguments citing safety, security and other concerns were not supported by sufficient evidence”.

It added: “The Panel unanimously concluded that, in the light of the applicable IIHF regulations, only substantiated security concerns could outweigh athletes of a particular nationality to participate in competitions. Consequently, the appeal was upheld.”

Its decision “did not order alternative measures, such as a neutrality regime, nor discussed organizational consequences” since they “were not requested and not subject to the appeal”.

Russia was exiled from sport following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine but some sports – including swimming and diving, table tennis, climbing, judo and taekwondo – have welcomed it back into the fold.

Russia remains banned from European and world football, although Fifa president Gianni Infantino has hinted at lifting it and allowed a Russian team to compete in last month’s Under-15 World Cup.

Andy Burnham has said Poundland’s owners must work with the government on a “practical solution” to secure the future of its workers and shops.

The Prime Minister criticised Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owns the retailer, for failing to engage with the “viable propositions” which have been tabled by a number of bidders.

Downing Street’s intervention comes amid growing political pressure on Gordon Brothers, as figures from Labour and Reform UK have criticised the Poundland owner for the handling of its attempted sale of the company.

Burnham said: “[Gordon Brothers should] focus on the people in your employment. […] Come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions.

“They’re on high streets. They matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here. Sit down with us and let’s find it.”

On Tuesday, a Downing Street spokesperson said Gordon Brothers is “not acting in the best interests” of its 12,000 staff and 600 stores.

“Gordon Brothers need to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going. That’s the case,” they said.

Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds is due to meet with Gordon Brothers today while future of work minister Kate Dearden is set to hold talks with Poundland’s managing director and finance officer, Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, also on Wednesday.

Third solvent bidder emerges

Poundland’s owners turned down a solvent bid from Irish firm Martin Property Group because it did not offer up-front payment for a £30m loan which was inherited from the retailer’s previous owners, PepCo. 

Innovest, an Irish investment firm, had also tabled a solvent bid for Poudland. This offer proposed to pay for the £30m loan up front but it is not being considered because the bidder could not provide proof of funds. 

Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesman, told City AM on Monday that he has been offering support to multiple Poundland bidders as he hit out at “greedy” Gordon Brothers.

On Wednesday, it emerged that another bidder is proposing to buy Poundland as a going concern. Xyra Group Holdings, a little-known investment group which has never bought a retailer before, said it would pay £12.5m up front for the company, as first reported by ITV News.

The bid is being considered by Gordon Brothers, according to sources familiar with the matter, although Xyra will need to provide proof of funds and reassure Poundland’s owners over its lack of retail experience.

The government has faced pressure to intervene to secure the future of Poundland’s workers but shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on Tuesday that Labour should avoid an “interventionist” approach and instead cut costs for employers.

Poundland filed a notice to appoint administrators on Thursday last week, making it more likely that the company will be broken up between a horde of buyers.

Retailers including Lidl, Tesco, Iceland, B&M, The Range and Poundstretcher are among those hoping to pick up some of Poundland’s stores if the firm collapses. 

Gordon Brothers believes it has found buyers for about half of Poundland’s 600 stores but is racing against time to find homes for the remainder of its estate before the moratorium lapses next Thursday, sources said.

]]> 2474497Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Haigh refuses to say when Labour will ‘get welfare bill down’ https://www.cityam.com/haigh-refuses-to-say-when-labour-will-get-welfare-bill-down/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:58:49 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474489

Andy Burnham’s deputy Louise Haigh refused to say when Labour will “get the welfare bill down” while adding the government would aim to “invest in success” when asked whether more taxes would cover increases in the benefits bill. 

Haigh, who is referred to as the Prime Minister’s “enforcer” and stood in for Deputy Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday, batted away the Conservatives’ questions about the welfare bill. 

When asked by her opposite number Alex Burghart about whether she could rule out tax rises to cover a rise in working-age benefits spending, Haigh said: “We have been repeatedly clear that we cannot afford to pay for failure and must invest in success – and that is how we will bring the welfare bill down.

“We will make support more conditional on taking up opportunities, ensuring young people get help they need earlier, tackling the long-term drivers of welfare spending, including high housing costs, and we will do all this in a Labour way.”

Burghart accused the government of delaying reviews on welfare spending, including the Alan Milburn review on youth unemployment, as he pointed to official figures showing that the welfare bill would rise in each year of the parliament. Milburn is due to report on youth joblessness within weeks while the government will set out its full policy paper on welfare next year.

The Office for Budget Responsibility showed last week that total welfare spending would rise from around £334bn in 2025 to £413bn in 2030. The rise in expenditure is set to be largely driven by pensioner spending, with the triple lock on pensions driving up costs for taxpayers. 

The report showed that health and disability benefits for working age people could rise by a little less than £20bn while Universal Credit would jump by over £14bn. 

In parliament, Burghart said benefits spending totalled £183bn, which subtracts pensioner spending and adds up disability benefits with child benefits, Universal Credit and other spending. He pointed out that the sum was more than spending on defence, schools and policing combined. 

Burghart presses Haigh on welfare spending

Haigh accused the Tories of allowing the welfare bill to spike between 2010 and 2024 although she refused to set a date on when it would come down. John Healey came under scrutiny over comments suggesting that the welfare bill would come down before 2030. He clarified that spending would not fall before the next election. 

“It’s not correct to say that we’re going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that,” he told Channel 4 News. 

The government is also facing questions on whether it is aiming to bring the welfare bill down in absolute terms or as a proportion of current forecasts. 

Burghart said: “We all know what the Labour way is. The Labour way is more tax, more welfare and more borrowing.”

The City of London Corporation is defending allowing trans women to use female spaces at Hampstead Heath ponds, after it was accused by a feminist charity of compromising “privacy, dignity and a sense of safety”.

The charity Sex Matters is challenging the Square Mile authority’s rules the grant access to facilities at the North London swimming ponds in court on gender identity rather than sex in the High Court.

In June, the Corporation confirmed the Kenwood ladies pond would be accessible to transgender women, whose biological sex is male, while the Highgate men’s pond would be open to transgender men whose biological sex is female. The City of London confirmed the mixed pond would remain open to all.

In its written submissions, Sex Matters argues the policy violates the Equality Act 2010 and that allowing access to both biological women and trans women into the facilities “indirectly discriminates against women” by allowing biologically male users access on the basis of gender identity.

The charity said that for women using the ponds, “the particular disadvantage is the greater risk, compared to men, of experiencing compromise to their privacy, dignity and/or safety as a result.”

The City of London argued that the admission arrangement at the Hampstead bathing ponds is lawful under the Equality Act 2010.

“There is nothing in the Equality Act 2010 that supports the contention that trans-inclusive arrangements are inherently and necessarily unlawful,” it said.

Supreme court rules on gender identity

The case follows a Supreme Court judgment handed down in April last year in which the judges unanimously ruled that a woman is defined by biological sex.

Maya Forstater, chief executive of Sex Matters, said the charity “is asking the court to make a substantive judgment on whether any version of the City of London’s “trans inclusive” rules at the ponds are lawful.”

“We will also argue that allowing men who identify as women to use the Ladies’ Pond is a form of sex discrimination towards women, because their privacy, dignity and safety is compromised,” Forstater added.

A spokesperson for the City of London Corporation said: “The Supreme Court clarified the legal definition of ‘sex’, but it did not require all services to become single‑sex, nor did it prevent trans‑inclusive arrangements.

“Our focus is, and always has been, on providing a safe, respectful, and well‑managed environment for everyone who uses the ponds. We are confident that our approach is lawful, proportionate, and appropriate.”

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy has formally intervened in Sky’s £1.6bn takeover of ITV’s broadcasting business after raising concerns over its impact on media competition and the diversity of British news.

Nandy confirmed on Wednesday that she had issued a Public Interest Intervention Notice (PIIN), instructing the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and media regulator Ofcom to look into the proposed deal.

Both watchdogs have until 27 January to report their findings, after which Nandy will decide whether to order a more detailed investigation.

“Having fully considered their representations, I have decided to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice”, Nandy said.

It follows her warning last month that the merger could threaten freedom of expression and the diversity of views in news media.

Nandy also confirmed plans to extend existing media merger legislation to cover streaming services, bringing on-demand platforms under the same considerations as traditional broadcasting.

Sky and ITV face regulatory scrutiny

The proposed acquisition would see Sky take control of ITV’s Media and Entertainment division, including its TV channels and streaming platform ITVX.

ITV Studios, the production business behind shows like Love Island, has been excluded from the deal.

The companies have said that the merger would create a stronger British broadcasting business capable of competing with global streaming giants including Netflix and Disney+.

They expect around £200m in annual cost savings, largely through combining marketing and tech operations.

Sky has pledged to protect ITV’s free-to-air services and public-service broadcasting obligations, while keeping ITV News and Sky News editorially separate.

The CMA will assess competition and jurisdictional issues, while Ofcom will examine the public interest implications.

Conflict in the Middle East has plunged numerous sports events into uncertainty and this week caused organisers to shelve plans for the Saudi T100 in Jeddah on 27 and 28 November.

Scheduled races in Dubai on 14 November and Qatar, where the men’s and women’s T100 world champions are due to be crowned on 11 December, are still going ahead.

How Middle East conflict has played havoc with sport calendar

]]> 2474433Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres The parliamentary bill that could speed up the FCA https://www.cityam.com/the-parliamentary-bill-that-could-speed-up-the-fca/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:44:52 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474391

It may not be as glamorous as performative rule-cutting, but the Financial Services and Markets Bill has the potential to speed up the FCA, write Omar Salem and James Borley 

The British famously love queuing. And remember the outcry when some were accused of jumping the queue to see Queen Elizabeth II lying in state? Queuing isn’t just a tradition but says something about our sense of fairness.  

But we have all been in a situation where the queue isn’t moving, no one knows what’s happening and we start thinking about giving up. Too often that is the case for applicants for FCA and PRA licences, some of whom may go to other countries. 

Ask anyone who has tried to launch a payments firm or buy a broker what slows them down, and the answer is rarely the rules. It is the wait – unsure when the regulator will decide, or even when it will start deciding.

Granted, things have improved from the backlogs of a few years ago, and the FCA has become more proactive in explaining the process and its expectations to the market, but the process still takes too long and lacks accountability. 

The regulators’ favourite loophole

A key example of the lack of regulatory accountability in the system is the, at best, liberal interpretation of the law that the regulators have been using to massage their performance statistics. 

The clock for regulators to decide an application only starts ticking when it is ‘complete’. ‘Incomplete’ has become a convenient way for the FCA and PRA to buy more time, regardless of whether it is warranted or not. 

To complicate things further, the FCA also says it can choose to treat an application as ‘not been received’ because it does not include the ‘minimum information’ required. So, what is the difference between an application rejected for not having the ‘minimum information’ and one that is incomplete? Yes, you’re not alone in being confused.

The bill we need

The Financial Services and Markets Bill, which is currently making its way through Parliament, would make some limited decreases to deadlines that the regulators need to meet. This is part of the government’s ‘growth agenda’ and efforts to cut red tape. The bill would cut the maximum period for determining an authorisation from a year to… 10 months. The incompleteness loophole would be retained. We can do much better.

For starters, the bill should go further on deadlines and bring approvals for M&A within them. There is no reason why a maximum six-month period to determine an authorisation application should not be possible. The bill should set clearer standards that can’t be gamed on when an application is complete, while letting regulators more easily turn away poor-quality applications quickly.

The FCA should also be encouraged to learn from the firms it authorises. A single application can involve the applicant, its lawyers, several case officers and specialist teams at the FCA. Fintechs coordinate exactly this kind of multi-party work every day, using project management tools such as Jira to assign tasks, track dependencies and show everyone where things stand. Why can’t the FCA do this?

Imagine an applicant able to see that its file is with the financial crime team, that two questions are outstanding and that a decision is on track. Fewer chasing emails, fewer surprises and a clear record of where delays arise that can be used to find ways to improve the process. Agentic AI opens even more possibilities. The bill should require the regulators to report to Parliament on how they are making authorisations more efficient, including by using technology.

Fairness not favours

While there can be a trade-off between risk and growth, there are also many steps the FCA could take to support growth without increasing risk. Faster and more consistent authorisations are a prime example of this. This isn’t about lowering the standard of applications or giving favours to the City, but building a system that works. It may not be as glamorous as performative rule-cutting, but it would make a difference. What is more, like queuing, an accountable and effective authorisations process is a matter of fairness. 

Omar Salem is a partner consultant at Pierson Ferdinand UK LLP. James Borley is director for payment services and digital assets at Complyport

]]> 2474391 Omar Salem Omar Salem Canva announces sweeping job cuts after ‘hardest year yet’ https://www.cityam.com/canva-announces-sweeping-job-cuts-after-hardest-year-yet/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:25:02 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474354

Design software giant Canva has announced a sweeping restructuring affecting more than a fifth of its global workforce, as slowing growth and mounting AI costs put pressure on the Australian tech company.

The shake-up will affect 1,271 employees, equivalent to 22 per cent of its workforce, through redundancies, relocations and changes to existing roles.

Co-founder and chief executive Melanie Perkins described the decision as “without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history”, warning that the company needed to overhaul its operations to remain competitive as AI transforms the creative software industry.

“It has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade”, Perkins told staff on Wednesday. “Success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next”.

The company has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs or which countries will be most affected.

The restructuring follows a sharp slowdown in growth and a decline in Canva’s valuation, as investors question how traditional software businesses will compete with increasingly powerful AI tools.

AI costs mount as growth slows

Canva, founded in 2013, has grown into one of Australia’s most valuable technology companies by offering accessible design tools for presentations, marketing materials and social media content.

But the rise of generative AI has created both opportunities and challenges for the business, allowing users to generate graphics and other creative content while increasing competition from rival platforms.

Canva has invested heavily in developing its own AI features, although the cost of running advanced models has reportedly forced it to slow the rollout of some products.

Second-quarter revenue rose 25.2 per cent to $921.9m, but fell short of internal expectations, while the company reportedly lowered its growth forecast to around 20 per cent.

Earlier this year, investors Blackbird Ventures and Airtree reportedly marked down Canva’s valuation from approximately A$60bn (£31.1bn) to A$49bn, reflecting concerns about slowing growth and the cost of AI investment.

Perkins said the company needed to return to smaller teams with greater responsibility, reducing management layers and simplifying its operations.

“New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use”, she said.

Affected employees will receive at least six months’ salary, alongside career support and continued healthcare benefits where available.

Canva is also offering $10,000 grants to departing staff who want to launch businesses or community projects.

The restructuring comes amid a wider wave of job cuts across the technology and professional services industries, as businesses seek to reduce costs while investing in AI.

On Tuesday, Virgin Media O2 confirmed plans to cut thousands of UK jobs as part of an £800m cost-saving programme, including greater use of AI in customer service and network operations.

Thousands of UK workers are set to face an effective 64 per cent tax rate on their cash savings under a fresh tax raid launched by John Healey in his maiden Budget.

The Chancellor confirmed he will hike taxes on savings by a further two per cent in April 2027, taking the rate to 44 per cent and 49 per cent for higher and additional rate taxpayers respectively.

He also maintained the frozen tax thresholds implemented by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, including the longstanding personal allowance taper. If a worker’s income exceeds £100,000 the tax-free personal allowance is reduced by £1 for every £2 earned over the limit.

For employees paying 40 per cent income tax on their salary, this clawback adds a further 20p of tax for every £1 of interest received. 

Brits caught in the taper pay an effective 60 per cent marginal rate on savings interest above their allowance, but the incoming tax hike will see this penalty rise to 64 per cent.

Tax trap paradox

For Britain’s highest earners the measure creates far less distortion compared to those who find themselves close to the threshold.

Workers earning £200,000 have their personal allowance completely wiped out by their salary alone. This means additional savings interest cannot trigger any further tax clawback, leaving them to be taxed solely at the flat 49 per cent rate.

Instead workers on the lower end of the bracket, typically dubbed high earners not rich yet (HENRYs) are instead expected to bear the brunt of the increase.

HENRYs earning £110,000 land directly in the taper zone with a £500 personal savings allowance.

Every pound of savings interest above the £500 triggers the 44 per cent higher-rate savings tax while simultaneously stripping away 50p of their personal allowance.

The lost allowance exposes an extra 50p of salary to 40 per cent income tax, creating the “punishing” 64 per cent effective marginal rate and putting the rate they face 15 percentage points higher than someone earning nearly double their pay.

Michael Healy, chief executive of IG consumer, said: “The £100,000 threshold has become one of the most punishing features of Britain’s tax system. 

“Years of frozen thresholds have dragged more working professionals into its grip, and the Chancellor has now tightened the squeeze.”

Childcare cliff edge

The tax hike puts further pressure on HENRYs, including those who have lost their free childcare hours upon surpassing the £100,000 earnings threshold.

In dual households, individual salaries are taken into account meaning childcare hours are taken the moment one parent crosses the £100,000 line regardless of what the other earns.

Over 90 per cent who have crossed the threshold have argued it has left them unable to build long-term wealth or invest, according to IG.

More than half said they would invest more if crossing the threshold did not cost them free childcare.

“Higher taxes on savings risk undermining efforts to encourage more people to invest,” said Healy.

“Families already struggling with punitive tax rates and the loss of childcare support will have even less disposable income to put towards building long-term wealth. The result is a tax system that makes it harder for people to get ahead financially.”

While home secretary Shabana Mahmood’s climbdown over her settlement reforms will delight some within her own party, it will disappoint many who believed that the Burnham Government would address growing public concerns over sensitive matters of immigration, integration, and identity.

Mahmood’s initial plans for migrant care workers already in the UK to wait 15 years for permanent settlement were previously labelled by former deputy prime minister and current housing secretary as “un-British”, with energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh hesitating to express support for the reforms in a recent interview. Under the watered-down plans, if care workers earn at least £25,000 a year and entered the UK before May 2025, they will be eligible for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years – sparing 282,000 migrants from delayed settlement.

Quality and quantity

The climbdown will not only reinforce public anxieties over the lack of quantity and quality control when it comes to the UK’s lax immigration system – it is likely to cost British taxpayers billions of pounds. Having ILR, migrants gain a suite of rights and benefits, such as being able to work without restrictions and having access to public funds. Moving from ‘pre-settled status’ to having ILR means that migrants may become eligible to apply for social housing (on the grounds of meeting the council’s requirements based on length of residency in the local authority area and need). Migrants with ILR are exempt from paying the Immigration Health Surcharge (HIS), therefore entitled to free access to NHS hospital treatment on a similar basis to that of an ordinarily resident person. A variety of welfare benefits are available with ILR (with conditions depending on the type of state assistance), as well as council tax reductions. Mahmood is currently refusing to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

There is also the worry that reversing the decision to extend the period before migrant care workers qualify for ILR, means that the UK Government is unwilling to implement a comprehensive skills, training and pay strategy for the sector to make jobs more attractive for domestic workers. As Policy Exchange argued in its Double Vision report in relation to medics, the UK must stop relying so heavily on overseas recruitment and should instead focus on finding ways to attract domestic workers into healthcare professions. 

The reality is that care roles are both mentally challenging and physically demanding. As it stands, British citizens who are entertaining entering the care professions are simply not provided with the training support, sufficient pay, and favourable working conditions they deserve – ultimately because the sector has been flooded with foreign care workers who are generally accepting of low wages and superficial rights. There are also questions regarding the overall level of English language proficiency among migrant workers who arrived after the January 2021 post-Brexit liberalisation of visa rules – which in turn feeds into concerns over the quality of care for service users, especially elderly people who speak specific local dialects. The reckless internationalisation of care in the country is a national scandal.

But there is a broader-picture problem here – what kind of state do we have and what type of society do we now live in? One of the most pro-family measures any government could take is phasing out care visas completely. The sorry model of private care homes profiting from a cultural individualism where familial caring responsibilities are outsourced to cheap foreign labour should be rejected – especially by a Labour government with a supposedly socially conservative home secretary. Instead, it has now been consolidated by the state. The current government has missed a golden opportunity to send a signal that the UK is committed to a national care approach centred on a motivated domestic workforce and the encouragement of within-the-family support except for the very most serious mental and physical conditions.

Dr Rakib Ehsan is a senior fellow at Policy Exchange.

    In the film My Fair Lady, the heroine’s father, Alfred P Doolittle, makes a memorable case for charity to the undeserving, including himself. His needs, he explains, are every bit as great as the most deserving widow’s – but, as he puts it: “if there’s anything going, and I put in for a bit of it, it’s always the same story: ‘You’re undeserving, so you can’t have it.’”

    The new relief – a 10 per cent rate of capital gains tax on up to £10m of lifetime gains – is designed to encourage and reward founders. The draft rules are narrowly drawn. A claimant must have held at least 25 per cent of the ordinary shares and votes when trading, or preparations for it, began. They must have held them for five years, and been a UK resident for five continuous tax years. Broadly, the company needs £10m of turnover and 15 full-time staff, plus two of three tests: 25 per cent compound annual growth over three years in turnover, the same in headcount, or recent R&D relief claims on £1.5m of spending.

    The intention is that only genuine founders or early investors in the most exceptional “high-growth, innovative” companies qualify. Everyone else is, by implication, undeserving. Which raises the question: who, exactly, does the government think deserves it?

    If there is one kind of company the government should want founded – and kept – in the UK, it is a frontier artificial intelligence lab. Leaving aside the requirements linked to UK residence, consider how the rules would apply to one: Anthropic, which has just filed for a Nasdaq listing.

In fact, since no more than four people can each own a quarter of anything, no company can ever have more than four deserving founders. Other founders of AI companies are equally undeserving. OpenAI began life as a non-profit, so the most any of them could have held was a quarter of nothing. In a more transactional world, where the velocity of partner moves is increasing, partnerships are more brittle than they appear.

    By any metric Weil in 2026 was spectacularly successful with profits per equity partner of roughly $5.6m. Its demise has been well covered in the media but arguably its key problem was that it was beginning to lose ground to a number of its rivals and certain of its top rainmakers had looked for pastures new. The fact that a leading bankruptcy firm is now looking at a wind down is a notable irony

    The October 2026 dissolution of Weil, Gotshal & Manges makes the fragility vivid. I often worked alongside Weil in my career and whilst established almost 100 years ago they made their presence felt in the London market in the High Yield bust of the early 2000s, acting for many of the High Yield issuers at the time which were experiencing financial difficulties. They were the leading bankruptcy firm in the world in the early 2000s, establishing a storied relationship from blow ups such as Enron. By any metric Weil in 2026 was spectacularly successful with profits per equity partner of roughly $5.6m.

    Its demise has been well covered in the media but arguably its key problem was that it was beginning to lose ground to a number of its rivals and certain of its top rainmakers had looked for pastures new.

    The fact that a leading bankruptcy firm is now looking at a wind down is a notable irony.

    What makes the episode shocking is that it was not a story of a liquidity squeeze, which is usually the way firms go down. Their position was about as far from my typical distressed client as could be. Relative underperformance against faster-growing peers created vulnerability, but the terminal event was a loss of confidence and cohesion among the partners themselves. Once the run began, profitability and history were irrelevant. The assets really did take the elevator down every night, the trouble being that some of them were not showing up the next day.

    Their downfall was a classic run which mirrors a bank run. One high-billing partner leaves and the remaining partners immediately worry about diluted profits. A few more departures intensify the anxiety. Those still inside begin to fear being left holding the baby – responsibility for the firm’s liabilities, lease obligations and residual costs once the revenue has walked. The rational response is to get out first and extract one’s capital while it still exists.

    In much of ‘Big Law’ the old dynamics of collegiality and loyalty have largely given way to a transactional culture: maximise profits or move on. Firms themselves frequently eject partners who underperform. The “made it for life” model has been replaced by a professional-sport standard in which you are only as good as your last quarter. The incentive is to move first.

    In an interesting article Why Law Firms Collapse, Professor John Morley of Yale Law School argues that the partner structure is susceptible to creating the run dynamic, and that external investors could absorb losses and reduce the incentive to flee.

    His point doesn’t resonate with me. A law firm has no permanent asset base equivalent to Amazon’s code or logistics network. Amazon lost money for years while building durable value; patient capital allowed it to survive. No law firm could endure that. Law firms tend to pay out most of their profits every year – they are maximising-profits-now structures.

    UK law firms moving closer to US model

    Attractive as Morley’s argument is, most firms still operate on an hourly-rate, personal-exertion model. Bringing in outside investors would not change the Pareto reality (the so-called 80/20 rule) which holds that roughly 80 per cent of outcomes come from 20 per cent of people. In most firms a small number of partners generate most of the revenue. If those people leave, they leave a gaping hole in the firm’s finances. Top billers will not subsidise outside capital when they can cross the street to a traditional peer firm and keep a higher share of their own yield.

    UK partnerships have historically enjoyed greater structural resilience than US firms because reasonable restrictive covenants and bad-leaver provisions in partnership agreements are more readily enforceable, and because UK insolvency law does not impose the automatic clawbacks that incentivise US partners to flee at the first sign of trouble. Culturally, my observation is that US firms seem to encourage the buccaneering ‘gun slinger’ spirit of the energetic rainmaker whereas UK firms tend to be somewhat better at institutionalising clients somewhat at the expense of a more dynamic US approach. Thus, UK firms make for a more stable environment. Even so, large UK commercial firms face intense pressure competing with US firms that have deeper pockets and operate in the world’s most profitable legal market.

    The bigger UK firms whilst remaining of top-notch quality have significantly lower partner profits and thus are vulnerable to the lure of higher compensation packages.  Outside competition has engendered a similar loss of loyalty.

    Faced with that competition, many UK firms have moved closer to the US model arguably at the expense of collegiality. Traditional lockstep, under which partners progressed largely by seniority, has given way to modified systems that award “super points”, for star performers. The shift rewards rainmakers and helps retain talent against US offers, but it also reinforces the transactional culture in which partners are only as valuable as their current contribution.

    This makes the government’s proposals to restrict non-compete clauses a live question. The recent announcements focus on employment contracts and the need to support innovation and mobility. It remains unclear whether any legislation will be limited to employment contracts or will also reach LLP agreements and partnership arrangements. Genuine partners contract as co-owners rather than employees, so reforms aimed only at employment relationships may not affect them. Given Weil’s example the UK government would be wise to leave equity partners out of the proposed restrictions.

    City firms could be facing a volatile future

    Weil’s collapse which is the biggest law firm failure in history offers a concrete warning. A highly profitable, debt-light firm still unravelled once partner confidence broke and high-billing lawyers walked. If the government extends any restriction to equity owners in professional firms, it will remove one of the few contractual tools that currently give UK partnerships greater resilience than their US counterparts. Do we really want the legal framework governing City law firm partnerships to move closer to the American model?

    An explicit carve-out for partner and LLP members – or at least confirmation that the rules will not reach partnership agreements – would preserve the contractual scaffolding that keeps London’s professional services sector more stable. Without it, City firms could face the same hyper-volatile lateral dynamics that have just felled a storied American institution.

    Yet even the best structure has limits. Whatever the ownership form or covenant architecture, if the partners do not like each other, cannot agree on fundamental strategy, or are on a losing path, no technical fix will save the firm. Structures can slow a run and cushion its effects; they cannot manufacture the underlying partnership that makes a firm durable in the first place.

    Stephen Phillips is a partner at FreiLibertas Law and host of The Turnaround Podcast

    Is the boss of PwC right that working from home is holding back young people? We hear the case for and against in this week’s Debate

    YES: Two fifths of young workers say home working is restricting their development

    Home and hybrid working can provide valuable flexibility and improve work-life balance. But these benefits are not always experienced equally, with younger workers potentially missing out on the workplace relationships and informal learning that more established professionals have already developed.

    Research conducted by the Institution of Occupational Safety and Health (IOSH) last year found almost half (48 per cent) of 18 to 24-year-olds said home and hybrid working made it harder to build relationships with colleagues and managers. More than two-fifths, 43 per cent, feared that fewer face-to-face interactions were restricting their personal and professional development.

    Too often, the problem is not flexibility itself but a lack of structured support. Only 19 per cent of 18 to 24-year-olds received constructive feedback two or three times a week.
    Working from home can hinder young peoples’ development when employers treat flexibility as a substitute for active management, though an inflexible return-to-office mandate is not, by itself, the answer.

    Simply requiring young people to be physically present in a workplace does not guarantee meaningful learning, effective supervision or career progression. What matters is whether employers are deliberately creating opportunities for people to develop, build relationships and feel part of their organisation. Theoretically, this can happen anywhere (remote or in person), but in practice management and development structures may not always provide this support as consistently in a remote or hybrid environment.

    Kelly Nicoll is the former president at IOSH

    NO: Flexibility is what makes work possible for a growing number of young people

    PWC boss Marco Amitrano is right that young people need employers to actively engage them. Our evidence shows that mentoring, proximity and unplanned, everyday conversations are among the most important benefits of in-person time, especially in someone’s first years at work. Employers also tell us it’s harder to integrate young people when senior managers work remotely. But the answer isn’t to send everyone back to the office. It’s to design hybrid working properly.

    The wider evidence on hybrid working is positive. Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom finds no productivity penalty from well-structured hybrid working, and real gains in retention, especially for women and staff with long commutes.

    Get it wrong, and you lose people. Flexibility is what makes work possible for a growing number of young people with mental health conditions, for the 5.5m disabled people in work, and for older workers approaching retirement.

    The best employers are already showing how. Instead of blanket mandates that could cost them their best staff, they’re building in structured mentoring, deliberate team days and managers equipped to bring new starters in, wherever they work.

    The Employment Rights Act’s new approach to flexible working requests is a chance to make that the norm. This isn’t a choice between flexibility and young people’s development. It’s a chance for employers to get it right, for young people and for everyone else.

    Clare McNeil is the CEO of non-profit business consultancy Timewise

    THE VERDICT

    The UK boss of PwC, Marco Amitrano, this week spoke out about the negative consequences of work-from-home policies, which he believes (while brought in with “good intentions”) are now holding young people back: “Once you’ve said ‘just go home’ then it’s out of sight and out of control.”

    Complaining about the shortcomings of the young in the workplace is nothing new, but could Amitrano have a point on this one? After all, it has been reported that Gen Z workers are no longer equipped in basic office skills like picking up the phone.

    While it’s logical, as Ms McNeil argues, to say that blaming the setting rather than the surrounding support structures for inadequate work can be a lazy approach (bad management is bad management wherever it is), it is also true there is a practical difference between the accountability of work done at home versus in the office – and we all know it! The verdict: realistically, remote work will never deliver the same development as good in-person management can.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.
