]]> EU-Startups has received exclusive investment data directly from our partners at the European Innovation Council (EIC), revealing the ten companies that secured the largest EIC Fund commitments during the first three quarters of the year.

From quantum computing and nuclear fusion to biotechnology and space technology, the total 85 investments made by the EIC in 2026 offer a closer look at where European public investment is flowing – with the top 10 representing the forefront of European innovation.

We’ve ranked the companies by their total EIC Fund commitments signed between January and September 2026, combining multiple investments in the same company and outlining EIC contributions from larger funding rounds involving other investors. Here are the ten biggest recipients so far!

The European Champions

€34.5 million

EnduroSat (Bulgaria): Founded in 2015 by Raycho Raychev, EnduroSat is a Bulgarian SpaceTech company making satellite technology accessible and affordable. The startup designs, manufactures and operates satellites, offering a satellite-as-a-service model that allows clients to deploy space missions without developing their own spacecraft.

Its €34.5 million EIC commitment was signed on 17 August 2026. The company subsequently announced a €182 million ($205 million) funding round in September, with the EIC among its backers.

€33.3 million

Reverion (Germany): Founded in 2022 as a spin-off from the Technical University of Munich, Reverion is developing reversible power plants that can generate electricity from gases such as biogas and hydrogen, while also converting surplus electricity into storable fuels. The company is working to make renewable energy available when solar and wind production cannot meet demand. Its EIC commitments total €33.3 million across two investments signed in June and August 2026.

EU-Startups covered Reverion’s €154.2 million Series B round in September 2026, which included participation from the EIC Fund alongside Kembara, Allianz, KfW Capital and other investors.

€30 million

Pasqal (France): Founded in 2019, Paris-based Pasqal develops quantum computers powered by neutral atoms manipulated using lasers. Its technology aims to tackle complex calculations in areas such as materials science, optimisation and pharmaceutical research. The company was co-founded by a team including Alain Aspect, the 2022 Nobel Prize winner in Physics.

Pasqal secured an EIC Fund investment of almost €30 million on 30 January 2026, when it was still a privately held quantum computing scaleup. The company subsequently went public on Nasdaq in August 2026, marking a significant milestone in its growth.

Focused Energy (Germany): Founded in 2021, Darmstadt-based Focused Energy is working to turn nuclear fusion into a commercially viable electricity source. The company uses powerful lasers to compress and heat fuel, pursuing a fusion process that could eventually generate electricity without the carbon emissions associated with fossil fuels.

The German-American startup secured an EIC commitment of almost €30 million in May 2026. That same month, it announced a €213 million ($240 million) Series A, with investors including RWE, SPRIND, Prime Movers Lab and the EIC Fund. The company aims to develop a laser-fusion power plant in Biblis, Germany, during the 2030s.

€25 million

SMART Photonics (The Netherlands): Founded in 2012 and headquartered in Eindhoven, SMART Photonics manufactures photonic integrated circuits, chips that use light to transmit and process information rather than relying exclusively on electrical signals.

Its indium phosphide technology has applications in telecommunications, data centres, artificial intelligence infrastructure and sensing. The company operates as an independent manufacturer, allowing customers to develop their own chip designs without building fabrication facilities.

SMART Photonics secured €25 million from the EIC Fund in May 2026. The investment comes as the company participates in efforts to expand European photonic chip manufacturing, including a new six-inch wafer pilot line in Eindhoven.

€20 million

Leyden Labs  (The Netherlands): Founded in Amsterdam in 2020, Leyden Labs is developing nasal sprays designed to protect people against respiratory viruses, including influenza and coronaviruses.

Rather than relying entirely on traditional vaccination approaches, the company’s technology delivers broadly protective antibodies directly to the respiratory tract, where many airborne infections begin. Its research aims to develop protection against multiple viral strains, including emerging variants.

Leyden Labs received an EIC commitment of almost €20 million in April 2026. EU-Startups covered its €40 million funding round in June, which brought together the EIC Fund, Invest-NL, the Gates Foundation Strategic Investment Fund, ClavystBio and other investors.

€14 million

Quandela (France): Founded in 2017 near Paris, Quandela is building quantum computers that use photons, or particles of light, to process information. The company develops both the hardware behind these machines and the software infrastructure needed to make quantum computing accessible to researchers and businesses.

Its technology combines photonic processors, single-photon sources and cloud-based computing services. In April 2026, the company reached another milestone with the inauguration of Lucy, a photonic quantum computer installed at France’s CEA computing centre.

Quandela secured an EIC Fund commitment of almost €14 million in July 2026.

€12.5 million

AURA AERO (France): Founded in 2018, Toulouse-based AURA AERO is developing lower-emission aircraft, including electric training planes and hybrid-electric regional passenger aircraft.

Its product portfolio includes the INTEGRAL family of aircraft and ERA, a proposed hybrid-electric regional airliner. The company is also developing unmanned aerial systems as it works towards expanding production in Europe and the United States.

AURA AERO received an EIC commitment of almost €12.5 million in March 2026. In April, it announced a €50 million Series B round, backed by the EIC Fund, Bpifrance’s French Tech Souveraineté fund, Safran Corporate Ventures, Innovacom and other investors.

Quobly (France): Founded in 2022 in Grenoble, Quobly is developing silicon-based quantum computers using semiconductor manufacturing techniques. A spin-off from CEA-Leti and CNRS, the startup aims to make quantum processors easier to manufacture and integrate into existing computing infrastructure.

Its approach uses silicon qubits built with industrial semiconductor processes, potentially helping quantum computing move beyond specialised research environments.

Quobly secured an EIC Fund commitment of almost €12.5 million in May 2026. EU-Startups covered its €115 million Series A round in June, led by Bpifrance, SEALSQ and STMicroelectronics, with participation from the EIC and other investors.

Proxima Fusion (Germany): Founded in 2023 as a spin-off from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Munich-based Proxima Fusion is developing nuclear fusion power plants using stellarators, magnetic confinement devices designed to hold extremely hot plasma in place.

The company is working towards its Alpha demonstrator, a major step in testing the technologies needed for commercial fusion energy. Its longer-term ambition is to develop power plants capable of delivering electricity at scale.

Proxima Fusion secured an EIC commitment of approximately €12.48 million in July 2026. EU-Startups covered its €411 million financing round that same month, with participation from the EIC Fund alongside investors including XTX Ventures, East X Ventures, RWE and Google.

More Information

Together, these ten companies account for approximately €224.1 million in EIC Fund investment commitments signed during the first nine months of 2026.

Interested in learning more about the EIC? Watch our interview with Momchil Sabev, Director of the European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA).

Editor’s Note: Exclusive EIC Fund investment data shared with EU-Startups, covering Q1, Q2 and Q3 2026. Amounts have been rounded for readability, with rankings determined using the original commitment figures. These figures represent EIC Fund commitments rather than total funding rounds or confirmed cash disbursements.

]]> Women TechEU is a European Union initiative that supports the growth of women-led DeepTech startups across Europe. Between 2026 and 2028, the programme aims to support 160 startups through grants of €75,000 each, alongside mentoring, training, expert guidance, networking, and opportunities to connect with investors and other European funding programmes.

To extend this support beyond the programme itself, Women TechEU has created the Allies network, bringing together organisations that want to help women-led DeepTech startups grow. The network includes investors, technology companies, innovation organisations, media partners, EU projects, and public institutions.

Who are the Women TechEU Allies?

The Women TechEU Allies network brings together organisations from across Europe that can offer startups valuable connections, expertise, resources, and visibility.

Its members include investors such as Alma Angels, Antler, and Playfair Capital, which help connect startups with investment opportunities and funding networks.

Technology companies and ecosystem organisations such as Microsoft, FundingBox, Women in Tech, the Western Balkan Startup Alliance, allWomen, Impulse4Women, and WomenTechIceland contribute through mentoring, knowledge sharing, and access to entrepreneurial communities.

Media and event partners, including TechBBQ, Web Summit, and Wolves Summit, help increase the visibility of women-led DeepTech startups. European initiatives such as EIT Deep Tech Talent, PQreact, and Ready2Scale also participate, supporting collaboration and access to additional opportunities.

Together, these organisations help create a stronger network of support for women entrepreneurs across Europe.

What does being an ally involve?

Becoming a Women TechEU ally means joining this network and contributing to the growth of women-led DeepTech startups.

Allies can support startups in different ways, including offering mentoring, sharing business and funding opportunities, making introductions to investors or corporate partners, and promoting women-led innovations through their networks.

In return, Allies gain access to the Women TechEU Partner-Hub, an online platform where startups, investors, companies, and other ecosystem organisations can connect and collaborate.

Through the Partner-Hub and the wider network, Allies can:

  • Connect with women-led DeepTech startups and other European innovation stakeholders.
  • Participate in investment events, corporate challenges, meetups, and networking activities.
  • Receive a dedicated ally badge on their Partner-Hub profile.
  • Gain visibility through Women TechEU’s website and social media channels.
  • Receive a communications pack to help promote Women TechEU within their own networks.

How to become a Women TechEU ally

Joining the Allies network is a straightforward process.

First, interested organisations register on the Women TechEU Partner-Hub, the programme’s online networking platform. During registration, they simply select the option indicating that they would like to become an ally.

Within one week, the Women TechEU Helpdesk team contacts them with further information and a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). This is a document that sets out the collaboration between Women TechEU and the organisation.

Once both parties sign the MoU, the organisation officially becomes a Women TechEU ally and can take part in the network’s activities.

The Partner-Hub therefore serves two purposes: it is where organisations express their interest in becoming Allies, and it is also the online space they use to connect with startups and other members of the Women TechEU community.

By joining the Allies network, organisations can contribute their expertise, connections, and resources to help more women-led DeepTech startups access opportunities and grow across Europe.

Interested in becoming an ally? Visit the Women TechEU website to learn more and access the Partner-Hub.

Neither the European Union nor the granting authority can be held responsible for them.

The Women TechEU scheme is an EU-funded project supporting women leading deep tech startup companies from Europe. As part of the consortium team implementing the programme, our mission is to foster inclusive innovation by supporting women-led startups, including under-represented deep tech sectors and European regions. We believe that diversity drives innovation, and we are here to provide women in deep tech with more opportunities, resources, and support in order to build market-shaping companies at global level.

Between 2026-2028, the current project consortium will run a continuous open call with 4 cut-off dates. Following a rigorous evaluation process, 160 total beneficiaries will be selected. ]]> When Ireland’s Government recently announced Budget 2027, it focused on addressing a problem that has beset Ireland’s startup community for decades.

A €1 billion Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) scaling programme would seek to provide startups with greater access to growth capital. The need was made particularly stark after, in 2025, the Department of Enterprise grimly projected a €1.1 billion equity-financing gap for Irish enterprises by 2030.

The Budget recognised a problem that startups here have known about for years: Ireland is excellent at getting businesses started, but too many founders struggle to raise the money they need to scale and expand. 

Ireland’s scale-up funding gap

This is particularly the case for those seeking Series B investment and beyond. In fact, a 2026 survey from Scale Ireland shows that three-quarters of Irish startup founders find it difficult or very difficult to attract private capital.

Their response tends to be one of two options: sell to a foreign acquirer or move to bigger markets like the UK or US where there is a much larger pool of investors. And why wouldn’t they? It makes sense for the survival and growth of their company.

It does, however, raise a bigger question for Ireland: how do we help more companies grow internationally while keeping their roots here? 

Turning investment promises into action

The new ISIF programme is aimed at addressing the right issue, but its impact will depend on how it works in practice. What companies can access it, how will the money be deployed and on what terms, and how much process will founders have to navigate? These are the important questions that need to be answered with tangible solutions.

The proposed €1 billion is exciting, but only if the timing and application are right. In 2025, the European Commission revealed that Ireland performed below the EU average for innovation-friendly regulation, highlighting the need for better and clearer support infrastructures. Therefore, it is crucial to know if capital will be available at the point when a company needs it.

Budget 2027 also extends existing startup and small business investment schemes. Again, this is most welcome but also sort of a non-announcement. Of course we want these schemes to continue, but the extension does not address the underlying problems. In reality, processes remain complex, funds are slow to be administered and it is unclear who qualifies.

The Capital Gains Tax reduction from 33% to 31% is another positive signal. But a two-point reduction on its own is unlikely to close the scale-up funding gap. The wider goal should be to encourage more investment in Irish companies and give founders the confidence to reinvest in growth.

Growth requires more than capital

Founders need practical improvements: less time spent navigating national requirements, clearer processes and a more straightforward path to customers and investors in other member states. Europe has the scale to be a powerful growth market; it needs to work more like one.

Capital is vital, but it is not the only ingredient required for a growing company. Founders also need customers, experienced people, local knowledge and trusted connections. Starting a business can be lonely. A supportive community can help founders find advice, collaborators and opportunities through the conversations that happen when people spend time together.

Ireland has built a strong base of entrepreneurs and international connections. According to the European Commission, Ireland sits 7th of 27 EU member states on the European Startup and Scaleup Scoreboard, highlighting the potential in our competitive startup environment.

Helping Irish startups scale from home

The next task is to build the conditions that help more of those businesses raise later-stage capital and reach international markets from here. The Budget’s announcements are a start. Their success will be measured by whether companies can use the supports in time, whether private investment follows and whether more Irish businesses can scale without having to leave to do so.

]]> Biograil, a Copenhagen-based BioTech company developing an oral device to deliver therapeutics that would otherwise require injection, has closed a €20 million funding round.

The round was backed by Verve Ventures and Megatrend Invest. HTGF, which led the company’s Seed syndicate in 2019, participated through its HTGF Opportunity growth fund. In July 2025, the company announced the first close of an €8.5 million financing round led by Verve Ventures.

“We first invested in Biograil in 2019 because we saw the potential of its approach to oral drug delivery. Our participation through the HTGF Opportunity reflects our continued conviction in that potential as the company prepares for clinical development,” said Anke Cassing, Principal at HTGF.

Founded in 2019, Biograil says it leverages its proprietary BIONDD technology to transform the large market for injectable pharmaceutical products into convenient oral capsules.

According to the company, the BIONDD device is contained in a standard-size, double-zero or single-zero capsule that is easy to swallow. The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a device with a spring-loaded grabbing mechanism. The device then safely attaches to the stomach wall and releases medication into the tissue for systemic distribution. 

The Biograil device uses a novel mechanism to facilitate the delivery of biologics into the stomach wall, utilising a proprietary platform technology manufactured by injection moulding.  After the drug delivery, the bio-compostable device passes safely through the GI tract. 

Biograil CEO Karsten Lindhardt said, “Excellent to see such strong support from existing internal investors and involve the HTGF Opportunity growth fund in the round. This, in combination with non-diluting funding from partnerships, will enable Biograil to continue to move our BIONDD® technology toward Phase 1 clinical studies. 

“The BIONDD® technology can allow oral delivery of large market compounds for better convenience and medical benefit and, in addition, create development opportunities for new innovative combination products which may never have been feasible or attractive as conventional injectable or oral products”.

The company plans to use this capital to support the ongoing activities for the planned Phase 1 clinical testing of BIONDD® to achieve key milestones such as non-clinical GLP studies and establish manufacturing GMP process prior to a larger financing in 2027.

The Biograil team combines seasoned entrepreneurs with experience building successful BioTech companies and R&D executives behind the world’s first injection-moulded oral tablet approved by the FDA.

Its investor syndicate includes Megatrend Invest, Verve Ventures, High-Tech Gründerfonds, Eli Lilly and Co., Sanner Ventures, Evonik Venture Capital, Anobis GmbH and Roquette Ventures.

]]> The world’s biggest startup campus, STATION F, has revealed its top 40 companies for 2026, as well as announcing that STATION F companies have raised a record €2 billion in 2026 alone.

This is the 8th edition of the annual list, with 320 companies recognised to date. This year’s selected teams cover a variety of sectors, including AI and machine learning, DeepTech, infrastructure and developer tools, hardware and robotics, climate tech and more.

Founded by Xavier Niel in 2017 and based in Paris, the 50,000m2 campus supports over 1,000 startups a year, who take part in 40 different support programmes.

Every November since 2019, the STATION F Future 40 has named the most promising and best-performing startups on campus. The 2026 companies were chosen from over 1,000 startups at STATION F in 2026, which places them in the top 4% of all startups for this year.

Selection rests on strong metrics, traction and meaningful milestones, with no funding cap.

The list began in 2019 as a live pitch session on campus and moved online in 2020 so investors anywhere could take part. STATION F has also invested in select Future 40 teams since 2022 – including Pimento (recently acquired by Mistral) and Flowie (recently acquired by Sovos).

The 2026 Future 40 cohort is one of the better-funded cohorts and has raised €110 million to date. Arlequin AI (€28 million), CURA ($10 million), Cleavr (€8 million), Lemrock (€7 million) are amongst some of the funded teams.

From AICE’s underwater defence drones and Bleu Robotics’ humanoid robots to CURA’s cement decarbonisation technology and RainPath’s AI-powered cancer diagnostics, the cohort tackles challenges across defence, climate, healthcare and infrastructure. AI remains a dominant theme, with companies like Lemrock, NuMind and Arlequin AI developing applications spanning commerce, document processing and high-stakes decision-making.

Most of the companies are pre-Seed and Seed – 31 total, with and 2 at Series A. 5 companies are bootstrapped. Fourteen companies come from F/AI, and others joined through partner programmes run with CentraleSupélec, Microsoft, TotalEnergies, Entrepreneur First and HEC.

Across eight editions, Future 40 companies have raised a cumulative €1.2 billion. Past selections include Fintecture, Tomorro, Spore.bio, WhiteLab Genomics, Biolevate, Qevlar AI, Syntetica and more. Hugging Face and Mistral AI have both acquired Future 40 companies.

This momentum has been reflected in EU-Startups’ own coverage throughout 2026. We’ve reported on fresh funding for Cleavr (€1 million), Lemrock (€6 million), Qevlar AI (€25 million), Syntetica (26 million) and WhiteLab Genomics (€23 million), alongside Spore.Bio’s AI-driven research expansion and Multiverse Computing’s €500 million Series C – highlighting the breadth of innovation and investment emerging from the STATION F ecosystem.

In addition to the Future 40 selection, STATION F companies have raised a record €2 billion in 2026 alone – this surpasses the funding record set in 2025.

Since 2022, STATION F companies have raised more than €1 billion each year, with over €1.5 billion raised in 2025. Larger rounds from alumni such as Multiverse Computing (€500 million) and Alan (€480 million) helped set the new record.

]]> Glovo showcased its growing influence on Europe’s entrepreneurial ecosystem at its fourth annual Startup Campus, held at its Yellow Park headquarters in Barcelona. The event coincided with new research revealing that former Glovo employees have founded 35 startups with a combined estimated value of €461 million, highlighting the company’s success in fostering entrepreneurial mindsets and national innovation ecosystems.

Delivery Hero’s €7.5 Billion Founder Factory

According to the research, Delivery Hero ranks as Europe’s largest “founder factory” by number of startups created by former employees, ahead of companies including Klarna, Zalando and Spotify.

Glovo accounts for 35 of these businesses, demonstrating how experience gained at established technology companies can translate into new entrepreneurial ventures.

“When we started Glovo in Barcelona in 2015, we had to figure out the startup playbook the hard way,” said Glovo co-founder Sacha Michaud, emphasising the company’s commitment to sharing its experience with the next generation of founders.

Startup Campus aims to accelerate early-stage businesses by providing access to industry expertise, strategic partnerships and potential investors.

Participants attended masterclasses, workshops and mentoring sessions led by technology experts, including Glovo co-founders Oscar Pierre and Sacha Michaud. The programme was supported by Endeavor Spain, ACCIÓ (Generalitat de Catalunya) and the Polish Development Fund (PFR).

The campus concluded with a pitching competition judged by representatives from Endeavor, ACCIÓ, BBVA Spark and Encomenda Smart Capital, giving founders an opportunity to present their solutions and receive strategic feedback.

Romanian startup .lumen wins pitch competition

Romanian assistive technology startup .lumen secured first place in the final pitching competition for its AI-powered navigation glasses designed to improve independent mobility for people with visual impairments.

Portuguese startup Granter finished second, while Spain’s Bleecker Technologies took third place.

“We’re incredibly honoured. We are building a technology which potentially can be of immense use for Glovo and its customers,” said .lumen CEO Cornel Amariei.

All three winning startups will continue receiving mentorship and strategic guidance from Sacha Michaud.

Since its launch in 2023, Glovo Startup Campus has hosted 53 startups, organised more than 20 local Power Up competitions and, according to the company, reached more than 1,000 people through its wider programme.

The latest edition reflects Glovo’s efforts to extend its influence beyond its core delivery business, connecting emerging founders with the experience, networks and resources needed to scale internationally.

This year’s Startup Campus brought together 19 startups working across AI, e-commerce, logistics, FinTech and sustainability.

The round also saw participation from early-stage venture firm Haatch and a group of angel investors.

“Businesses of all sizes and across all sectors often rely on commercial finance for a multitude of reasons, but the processes involved in granting this finance are often largely manual, making the process inefficient and slowing down lending decisions. Its flagship product, FlowSpread, automates financial spreading by extracting income statements, balance sheet data, and cash flow figures directly from PDFs, tax returns, and bank statements, eliminating manual data entry.

It also offers a Bank Statement Analysis tool that adds an additional layer of intelligence, automatically categorising transactions across multiple accounts, reconciling them against submitted financials, and flagging risk signals such as unusual activity, cash flow volatility, or concentration risk.

Crediflow AI says its platform can reduce the process that could take several days to between 10 and 30 minutes. It is already in use by hundreds of credit professionals across the UK, Europe, and the United States, including clients such as AddWorking Capital and Iveco Capital.

“When every transaction requires hours of manual preparation, it affects how much business a lender can take on and which deals are worth pursuing. We built Crediflow to bring that workload down and give credit teams more time to understand the borrower and structure the financing,” he added.

Germany’s mika raised €6 million to develop its AI-native accounting and tax platform, while Belgium’s Dytto secured €1.5 million for an AI assistant supporting accounting firms. Together with Tallia, funding in this space during 2026 reached approximately €35.6 million in financing.

Founded in 2025 by school friends Jack Mander and Alexander Bartlam, Tallia combines experience in professional tax advisory with expertise in engineering and technology.

The founders established Tallia to address a challenge facing tax professionals: how to use generative AI to accelerate research and drafting without compromising the accuracy, traceability and professional judgement required when advising clients.

Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, Tallia has been designed around the requirements of tax practices, where answers must be supported by legislation, regulatory guidance and case law. Its platform uses a custom retrieval system to connect AI-generated responses with relevant tax authorities, helping advisers verify the information before incorporating it into client deliverables.

One of the platform’s central features is its ability to combine external tax knowledge with a firm’s internal expertise. By connecting to existing documents, contracts, templates and previous work, Tallia aims to enable advisers to produce research and drafts that reflect their organisation’s established practices and knowledge.

The technology also incorporates structured review workflows, allowing senior professionals to examine the reasoning and supporting evidence behind AI-generated work.

The platform supports workflows across Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, allowing tax professionals to incorporate AI-assisted research and drafting into familiar software. According to Tallia, its system can produce a fully cited first draft in an average of 30 seconds, while teams using the platform save an average of five hours per fee earner each week.

With its new funding, Tallia intends to expand adoption of its platform among tax and accountancy firms, helping professionals spend less time on repetitive research and initial drafting while retaining control over the advice delivered to clients.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. Here are 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore.

In Brief 5 min read
  • Three NASA astronauts cast electronic ballots from the ISS during the 2026 US midterm elections.
  • Space voting began in 1997 when astronaut David Wolf became the first American to vote from orbit.
  • Encrypted ballots travel via NASA's satellite network to county election officials on Earth.

There was no queue, polling official or ballot box when NASA astronaut Anil Menon voted in the US midterm elections on Tuesday. His polling booth was a small compartment aboard the International Space Station, orbiting Earth at roughly 28,000 kilometres per hour.

Menon was one of three American astronauts who cast their ballots from space on 3 November, using an electronic voting system that allows eligible crew members to participate in elections without returning to Earth.

The other two were NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins.

“Yes, you can even vote from space!” Menon wrote in a social media post. “All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials.”

Yes, you can even vote from space! All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials. https://t.co/hJCExQ2nKr

— Anil Menon (@astro_anil) November 3, 2026

The astronaut also shared a short video showing how he voted, offering a rare glimpse of an everyday civic responsibility being carried out in an extraordinary setting.

Wearing an “I voted” sticker, Menon showed viewers the personal crew compartment he had used as his polling booth.

“Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today,” he explained.

The process took place hundreds of kilometres above the United States, but the ballot was destined for the same election authorities responsible for votes cast by residents of Harris County, Texas.

It was a small personal moment in a mission devoted largely to scientific research, spacecraft operations and maintaining the orbiting laboratory.

The first ballot from space

Voting from space is not a new privilege. Its origins go back to 1997, when American astronauts began spending extended periods aboard Russia’s Mir space station.

At the time, astronauts assigned to long-duration missions faced a problem that most voters never encounter. They could be away from Earth for months, with no practical means of visiting a polling station or returning an absentee ballot through ordinary postal services.

Texas lawmakers addressed the issue by passing legislation allowing eligible residents travelling in space to vote while in orbit.

The connection with Texas was important. NASA’s Johnson Space Center, the principal training and mission-control facility for American astronauts, is in Houston. Many astronauts live in the surrounding area.

The legislation provided a way for those residents to exercise their voting rights even when their work took them far beyond the planet.

Later that year, NASA astronaut David Wolf became the first American to cast a ballot from space.

Wolf was aboard Mir, the Russian station that preceded the International Space Station as a major destination for long-duration human spaceflight.

His vote established a precedent that has continued through successive generations of astronauts.

When the ISS began supporting a permanent human presence in November 2000, the same basic principle carried over: an astronaut’s absence from Earth should not prevent participation in an election.

How does a ballot travel from space to Earth?

Although the voting process appears simple from the astronaut’s perspective, delivering the ballot requires several stages of communication.

The astronaut first arranges to vote absentee, working with the election authorities in the county where they are registered.

As with other Americans who are away from home, astronauts can use a Federal Post Card Application to request an absentee ballot. Election officials prepare an electronic ballot, which is made available to the astronaut through NASA’s communications systems.

The astronaut accesses the ballot using individual credentials, makes the selections and sends the completed document back to Earth.

NASA says the process is supported by its Space Communications and Navigation programme, known as SCaN.

The ballot travels through the agency’s Near Space Network, which provides communication and navigation services for spacecraft operating relatively close to Earth.

From the ISS, the electronic document is transmitted through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System.

These satellites allow the space station to exchange information with ground facilities without having to wait until it passes directly over a particular receiving station.

The ballot is relayed to a ground antenna at NASA’s White Sands Test Facility in New Mexico. It then travels to Mission Control at Johnson Space Center in Houston before being forwarded to the appropriate county election official.

Security is an essential part of the arrangement.

NASA says the ballot is encrypted and accessible only to the astronaut and the county clerk, protecting the confidentiality and integrity of the vote during transmission.

The system does not mean astronauts can simply vote in any election by sending an email from orbit. They must meet the normal eligibility requirements and complete the necessary absentee-voting arrangements.

The difference is that their ballot travels through a spacecraft communications network rather than a postal system.

A tradition that has continued for decades

Several NASA astronauts have exercised their voting rights during missions since Wolf’s pioneering ballot in 1997.

Kate Rubins voted from the International Space Station during the 2016 presidential election and again in 2020.

During the 2020 election, Rubins was photographed beside a makeshift voting booth aboard the station.

The photograph captured an unusual contrast: an American election being observed from a spacecraft surrounded by scientific equipment, cables and the machinery needed to sustain human life in orbit.

The Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum later highlighted her experience as an example of how astronauts remain connected with ordinary life while living and working far from home.

More recently, NASA astronauts Loral O’Hara and Jasmin Moghbeli cast electronic absentee ballots from the station in March 2024 while registered as Texas voters.

Their completed ballots were transmitted to Mission Control and passed to local election officials.

Menon’s vote in the 2026 midterms continues that tradition, but his video offers a more personal look at the process.

Instead of focusing on the communications infrastructure or the legislation behind the system, he showed viewers the place where he sat to make his choices.

The voting booth was simply his room aboard the station.

Three votes from the same spacecraft

Menon arrived at the ISS in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

Delaney and Watkins joined the orbiting laboratory in October on SpaceX‘s Crew-13 mission.

Their election-day participation meant all three American crew members aboard the station were able to vote despite being away from their home country.

Investigators have recovered parts of a Learjet 60‘s tail up to 3.8 miles from the site of Sunday’s fatal crash in Florida, confirming that sections of the aircraft separated before impact.

The Learjet 60, operated by Aurora Aviation under the Upper Jets name, crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday, November 1, killing all nine people aboard.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) disclosed the discovery during its 3 November press briefing as investigators continued examining the aircraft’s rapid descent near West Palm Beach.

The aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas at approximately 10:37 am Eastern Time, bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.

Investigators recovered most of the aircraft’s left elevator, a movable control surface on the horizontal tail that controls pitch, in three pieces between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the main crash site.

“Certainly it tells us that at least some components, some pieces of the aircraft, important pieces of the aircraft, separated before the impact,” NTSB board member Tom Chapman said. “What that means exactly in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet.”

He described the discovery as a “very significant bit of evidence.”

Investigators confirm tail components separated in flight

Asked whether the elevator could have broken away when the aircraft struck the ground, Chapman said, “The distance from the site indicates that it separated before impact.” 

“It seems implausible that it would have been a result of the impact. It would have separated before the impact.”

Investigators are examining whether losing the elevator contributed to the aircraft’s loss of control or whether forces acting on the aircraft during its descent caused the component to break away.

“Those are the two likely possibilities that we’ll want to examine,” Chapman said.

The NTSB has not determined when the elevator separated or whether the aircraft was already descending uncontrollably when it happened.

Asked whether excessive descent speed could have caused the aircraft to break apart, Chapman said: “That is certainly one possibility.”

He cautioned that the elevator might not have remained effective at the aircraft’s speed, even if it had remained attached.

Learjet crew reported turbulence, icing and overspeed

According to the NTSB’s first briefing, the crew reported moderate turbulence and manageable icing while flying at 35,000ft. The pilots requested permission to climb to 37,000ft after encountering precipitation. Less than 30 seconds after receiving clearance, the crew reported a descent, followed by a mayday call.

The crew then reported the aircraft was overspeed and descending. Later communications indicated a rapid loss of altitude. The aircraft crashed at approximately 12:51 pm.

The NTSB has not established whether the reported icing, turbulence or overspeed caused the loss of control.

“Weather is certainly a key focus of the investigation,” Chapman said.

Weather remains a focus of the investigation

Asked whether investigators had examined the aircraft’s maintenance history, including the condition of its weather radar, Chapman said that work was ongoing and there was insufficient information to draw any conclusions.

Investigators are also examining crew qualifications, aircraft maintenance records and operational information.

The NTSB has received dashcam footage and multiple eyewitness accounts that could help establish the aircraft’s condition during its final moments.

The NTSB say they expect to start investigating the crash crater today. Chapman told the press conference an unstable utility pole had been removed and added, “NTSB is working with local public works teams to begin water removal from the impact crater so our investigation in and around the crater can begin. We believe that will begin tomorrow [Wednesday] in terms of being able to access the crater.”

The investigation is still in its early stages, and the NTSB has not yet identified a probable cause of the tragic accident.

Record-breaking order strengthens Avolon’s Boeing partnership

According to the leasing firm, the 140-aircraft agreement represents “a major commitment to the Boeing 737 MAX family and provides Avolon with additional capacity to meet the evolving requirements of airline customers worldwide.”

Demand for the largest member of the 737 MAX family has increased considerably throughout 2026. Aircraft lessors have placed firm orders for more than 230 Boeing 737-10 aircraft during the year, approximately five times the total lessor backlog for the largest 737 MAX variant at the end of 2025.

For Avolon, the order provides an opportunity to capitalise on demand for larger single-aisle aircraft while benefiting from the operational flexibility of the Boeing 737 family.

Avolon CEO Andy Cronin said the agreement reflects continued demand for new-technology aircraft and strengthens the company’s long-term delivery pipeline.

He highlighted the 737 MAX 10’s combination of competitive operating economics and increased passenger capacity, noting that the aircraft is well positioned to support airline growth and fleet renewal throughout the next decade.

Cronin also emphasised the importance of Avolon’s longstanding relationship with Boeing, describing the latest agreement as another step in strengthening the partnership.

Boeing welcomed Avolon’s expanded commitment to the 737 MAX programme, highlighting the benefits the aircraft family offers airlines seeking to modernise their fleets.

Brad McMullen, Boeing’s Senior Vice President of Commercial Sales and Marketing, said Avolon’s growing and diversified 737 MAX portfolio would help airline customers introduce aircraft that reduce emissions and operating costs while improving route economics. He also pointed to the importance of fuel-efficient aircraft as airlines prepare for continued growth in global passenger traffic.

With strong long-term travel demand anticipated, Boeing believes lessors will play an important role in helping airlines access modern single-aisle aircraft capable of operating across a wide range of route networks.

Boeing 737 MAX 10: Capacity, range and operating economics

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 is the largest aircraft in the 737 MAX family and has been developed to provide airlines with additional passenger capacity while retaining the operational advantages of a single-aisle aircraft.

According to Boeing, the aircraft offers the best per-seat economics of any single-aisle aircraft. Key specifications include a passenger capacity of up to 230 passengers and a maximum range of approximately 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 kilometres).

Its additional seating capacity makes the 737 MAX 10 particularly attractive to airlines operating high-demand short- and medium-haul routes. The aircraft’s economics also provide operators with opportunities to increase capacity without moving into the widebody market.

For aircraft lessors such as Avolon, the 737 MAX 10 offers an opportunity to meet airline demand for larger narrowbody aircraft while maintaining exposure to one of the world’s most widely operated commercial aircraft families.

Growing demand for single-aisle aircraft

The order comes amid expectations of sustained growth in global air travel. Passenger traffic is projected to increase by approximately 4% annually over the next 20 years, encouraging aircraft lessors to expand and diversify their single-aisle portfolios.

The Boeing 737 remains a cornerstone of the global aircraft leasing industry, accounting for approximately 30% of all financed aircraft. Across the lessor market, orders for the 737 MAX family have now exceeded 1,450 aircraft, representing approximately 20% of Boeing’s total backlog.

These figures underline the importance of the 737 MAX programme to the leasing sector and demonstrate the continued appetite for modern, fuel-efficient narrowbody aircraft.

Avolon’s latest agreement positions the company to support airline fleet expansion and replacement requirements over the coming years, while further strengthening its relationship with one of the world’s leading commercial aircraft manufacturers.

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 nears entry into service

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 is the fourth and largest member of Boeing’s 737 MAX family. Its development was launched in 2017 in response to airline demand for a higher-capacity narrowbody aircraft capable of competing more directly with the Airbus A321neo and to replace the Boeing 757.

Although the aircraft shares much of its design and technology with the other 737 MAX variants, the MAX 10 incorporates modifications to accommodate its longer fuselage and increased passenger capacity.

One of the most significant certification considerations has been the aircraft’s updated landing gear design. The 737-10 features a semi-levered main landing gear arrangement designed to provide the necessary ground clearance during take-off despite its longer fuselage.

The aircraft’s certification programme also involved extensive flight testing and regulatory evaluation, including assessments of handling characteristics, systems integration, performance, and compliance with applicable airworthiness requirements.

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 was eventually certified on October 20, paving the way for its entry into service with several airlines. WestJet, Ryanair, Alaska Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines are all preparing for Boeing’s largest 737 MAX variant, with WestJet likely to be the first recipient.

The US Air Force should reconsider plans to continue buying Boeing KC-46A tankers and invest instead in a new generation of blended-wing-body aircraft capable of carrying more fuel over much greater distances, according to a new study that challenges the service’s long-term aerial refuelling strategy.

The Hudson Institute report argues that a medium-sized blended-wing-body (BWB) tanker could refuel more than twice as many groups of combat aircraft as the KC-46A, or support them at more than twice the distance. It also estimates that acquiring and operating 250 such aircraft could save $15.5 billion over 30 years compared with an equivalent fleet of KC-46As.

Published on 27 October, the report, Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations, was written by Hudson Institute researchers Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin.

Their argument is straightforward: replacing old tankers with more aircraft of similar range may not solve the Air Force’s future refuelling problems.

“The medium-range KC-46A has performed well in contemporary operations and would play an important role in any conflict,” the researchers acknowledge.

But they conclude that the aircraft lacks the range, fuel delivery capacity and survivability needed to sustain large-scale operations across vast distances, particularly when tankers must operate from bases far from the aircraft they support.

The recommendation is an independent research proposal, not an official Air Force procurement opinion.

Why aircraft shape matters

A conventional tanker has a long cylindrical fuselage with wings attached. A blended-wing-body aircraft takes a different approach, merging the fuselage and wings into a broad, continuous lifting surface.

The shape reduces aerodynamic drag and improves efficiency, potentially allowing an aircraft to carry substantial fuel loads over longer distances without consuming as much fuel itself.

That distinction matters enormously in aerial refuelling.

A tanker must burn fuel to reach its assigned refuelling point, transfer fuel to other aircraft and retain enough to return safely to base. The farther it flies, the less fuel remains available to deliver.

The Hudson researchers found that this limitation becomes particularly severe when conventional tankers are required to support operations thousands of miles from their bases.

A purpose-built BWB tanker could change that calculation.

According to the study, the blended-wing-body tanker could deliver substantially more fuel than the KC-46A on long-distance missions. In some scenarios requiring large fuel transfers, the researchers calculated an advantage of up to five times.

That does not mean a BWB carries five times as much fuel in every situation. The advantage depends on mission distance and the amount of fuel required by receiving aircraft.

The researchers also examined the Airbus A330 MRTT+, but concluded that its somewhat greater range did not eliminate the same underlying limitations.

Fewer tankers could do more work

The report’s most striking findings concern how many aircraft would be needed to support a particular operation.

Using simulations of 32 mission scenarios across the Pacific, North America, Europe and the Middle East, the researchers compared the KC-46A, A330 MRTT+, medium BWB and two smaller tanker concepts designed to operate closer to potential threats.

Across the representative missions, the medium BWB required approximately 30% fewer aircraft than the KC-46A.

In one simulated deployment across the Pacific, moving an equivalent military force took 30 days using KC-46As but only 13 days with medium BWBs.

Another comparison examined the number of airfields capable of supporting sustained refuelling operations. Under one modelled scenario, the BWB could operate from 90 suitable airfields, compared with 31 for the KC-46A.

The difference is largely attributable to the BWB’s longer range, which would allow it to operate from more distant bases without relying heavily on other tankers.

That reliance is known as force extension. One tanker refuels another to increase the second aircraft’s reach. Although useful, the process consumes additional fuel and ties up aircraft that could otherwise support fighters, bombers or transport aircraft.

The researchers argue that a longer-range BWB could reduce this dependence and give commanders considerably more flexibility in choosing operating bases.

They also believe a dedicated refuelling aircraft could be cheaper to acquire and operate than a multi-role tanker such as the KC-46A, which is designed to transport passengers, cargo and aeromedical patients as well as fuel.

Those cost advantages remain estimates based on the researchers’ modelling rather than demonstrated performance from an operational BWB tanker.

JetZero offers a glimpse of what comes next

The Air Force has already taken steps to explore blended-wing-body technology.

In 2023, it awarded California-based aircraft developer JetZero a contract to build and test a full-scale BWB demonstrator in partnership with Northrop Grumman.

The aircraft is scheduled to make its first flight by the end of 2027.

Although JetZero’s demonstrator is not the specific tanker examined in the Hudson study, the programme could provide valuable evidence about the aerodynamic and manufacturing advantages of the configuration.

The Air Force’s interest reflects the potential applications of blended-wing technology beyond aerial refuelling, including military transport and commercial aviation.

JetZero is not alone in pursuing the concept.

Boeing, Airbus, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Natilus are among the manufacturers that have investigated blended-wing aircraft. Boeing’s earlier medium BWB concept provides the basis for the representative aircraft illustrated in the Hudson report.

The researchers note that improvements in aircraft design tools and composite manufacturing have made blended-wing configurations more economically practical than when the concept was first developed decades ago.

Commercial interest has also increased because of the potential to reduce fuel consumption and improve the economics of carrying passengers and freight.

A successful demonstrator, however, would be only one step towards an operational military tanker.

Such an aircraft would still need to accommodate aerial refuelling equipment, meet demanding reliability and maintenance requirements, and demonstrate that it can operate effectively from suitable military and civilian airfields.

Why the KC-46A is not being written off

The Hudson Institute is not calling for the immediate retirement of the KC-46A.

The Pegasus remains central to the Air Force’s tanker modernisation programme, and the report acknowledges its contribution to current operations.

Its concern is that continued purchases could eventually leave the service with a large fleet of aircraft that share the same fundamental range limitations.

The report notes that the Air Force plans to field at least 185 KC-46As, with the possibility of expanding the fleet to 260 or more through additional purchases.

It warns against allowing the convenience of continuing an established production programme to determine the composition of the future tanker fleet.

“A tanker fleet of KC-46As alone is insufficient to win in conflicts that require long-range, contested refueling operations,” the authors state.

Their alternative would involve reducing some planned KC-46A follow-on purchases and redirecting funding towards development of a medium BWB tanker.

One of the study’s proposed fleet plans, combining existing tanker procurement with the introduction of BWBs, was estimated to cost $15.5 billion less over 30 years than a plan relying exclusively on further KC-46A purchases. The researchers calculated that it would also provide 58% more fuel offload capacity.

The study argues that such a transition could be financed within projected annual funding levels, although developing an entirely new aircraft would introduce technical, financial and scheduling risks.

More than a question of buying new aircraft

The researchers also caution that even a more efficient tanker cannot solve every problem facing the Air Force.

Existing aircraft need better communications, situational awareness and defensive systems. Airfields require improved fuel storage, distribution facilities and protection against attack.

The study recommends that a future medium BWB be designed from the outset to accommodate advanced defensive equipment, potentially allowing it to operate somewhat closer to threats than conventional tankers.

This could reduce the distance fighters and other aircraft must travel to receive fuel, leaving more time and fuel available for their missions.

The proposed survivability advantages, however, depend on capabilities that have yet to be demonstrated on a full-scale BWB tanker.

The report also recognises a difficult procurement dilemma. Delaying the development of a new tanker would prolong dependence on the KC-135, some of which could approach 100 years of age before retirement under current projections.

Continuing to purchase KC-46As offers a more established route to replacing those aircraft, but could leave the Air Force facing the same operational constraints for decades.

The researchers believe the service should avoid making that trade-off by default.

Their findings do not establish that a blended-wing tanker is ready to replace the KC-46A. They do, however, present a case for developing one while the Air Force still has time to shape its future refuelling fleet.

In Brief 3 min read
  • White House Halloween Air Force One flyover triggered air traffic disruption around Washington, drawing criticism over planning and notification.
  • Senator Tammy Duckworth demanded answers from the FAA and Pentagon over the low-altitude presidential aircraft flyover.
  • The flyover reignited debate over public communication and the operational impact of presidential events.

A low-altitude flyover by the US presidential aircraft during a White House Halloween celebration has disrupted air traffic around Washington, D.C., delayed more than 200 commercial flights and prompted criticism over safety, planning and the limited warning given to the public.

The incident took place on Thursday, 29 October, as President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump hosted a Halloween event for children at the White House. The presidential aircraft made two passes over the White House and nearby neighbourhoods.

More than 200 commercial flights delayed

As reported by Reuters, the flyover prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to temporarily halt air traffic at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), one of the capital’s main airports.

According to flight-tracking service FlightAware, 202 flights were delayed on Thursday, representing 26% of departures and 17% of arrivals. Most of the delays were attributed to the temporary disruption associated with the aircraft’s passes over the city. Some passengers reported that their aircraft were forced to circle before landing, while others experienced delays to their journeys.

🇺🇸 The new Air Force One THUNDERS over the White House right in the middle of the Halloween party 🎃 Not sure the kids expected a presidential flyover with their candy 😅 Writer: Lucas https://t.co/RCAJMFzxLR

— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 29, 2026

The disruption highlighted the operational challenges of coordinating presidential movements around one of the busiest and most tightly controlled airspace environments in the United States.

Limited warning raises questions

One of the main criticisms concerned the short notice provided before the flyover. The District of Columbia Council said residents, officials at the Pentagon and personnel at the airport received only around 15 minutes’ warning. Airline representatives also reported having less than an hour’s notice.

The unexpected appearance of a large aircraft flying unusually low over the capital startled some residents. Washington has extensive airspace restrictions, and the incident prompted concerns about the risks associated with low-altitude flights in a densely populated area.

The White House promoted the manoeuvre on social media, describing it as an “epic Air Force One flyover” for children attending the Halloween celebration. The FAA, meanwhile, said the flight had been coordinated with the agency and that a temporary ground stop had been implemented at the airport.

Senator demands answers

The controversy escalated on 2 November, when Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth called for a full explanation from the FAA, the Pentagon and the White House Office of Management and Budget. Duckworth, who serves on a Senate subcommittee overseeing aviation regulation, questioned the flight’s purpose, cost, authorisation and safety arrangements.

She also raised concerns about the aircraft’s reported altitude, with flight-tracking data indicating that it flew at approximately 400 to 1,000 feet during its passes over Washington.

Duckworth asked officials to clarify whether the flight had been approved for training purposes, what objectives it was intended to achieve and what minimum altitude had been authorised. The FAA and Pentagon said they would respond directly to her questions.

The White House defended the event, stating that the FAA had followed the necessary safety protocols. It also argued that the flyover brought excitement to children attending the celebration and to others who watched nearby.

A spectacle with wider consequences

The aircraft is known as Air Force One whenever the US president is aboard. Presidential flyovers have previously taken place at major sporting events attended by Trump, but the Halloween appearance has drawn scrutiny because of its impact on airport operations and the questions surrounding advance notification.

Beyond the immediate flight delays, the episode has raised broader questions about how ceremonial displays involving presidential aircraft should be planned, communicated and coordinated with civilian aviation authorities.

With Senator Duckworth seeking further details, attention is now turning to the explanations provided by government agencies and whether any changes to procedures will follow.

What began as a Halloween spectacle at the White House has therefore become a wider debate about aviation safety, public communication and the responsibilities that accompany presidential events.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Shield AI has revealed X-BAT 001, believed to be its first flight-test vehicle, in a video showing the autonomous fighter’s airframe and markings.
  • Close-ups suggest its GE F110 propulsion hardware is installed, although Shield AI has yet to confirm the aircraft’s configuration and readiness.
  • Initial vertical takeoff and landing tests are targeted before the end of 2026, with production planned to begin in 2029.

Shield AI has offered a shadowy first look at X-BAT 001, believed to be the first flight-test vehicle for its autonomous, tail-sitting fighter aircraft.

A short video shows the aircraft inside a hangar, revealing its broad wings, digital camouflage and prominent engine exhaust. While the dramatic lighting conceals much of the detail, stills captured by Aerospace Global News offer a closer look at the aircraft taking shape.

AGN has asked Shield AI to confirm the vehicle’s status and configuration and is awaiting comment.

A closer look at X-BAT 001

The aircraft wears a grey digital camouflage scheme, broken up by dark edging and a contrasting central strip. “X-BAT 001” and “Powered by Hivemind” markings identify the vehicle and the autonomy software intended to fly it.

Its sharply swept wings blend into a substantial central body, with no cockpit or canopy. Panel boundaries and fasteners are visible in the closer views, alongside several upper-surface openings whose functions are not immediately clear.

Perhaps the most notable feature is the broad, mouth-like opening beneath the forward body. Appearing to form the aircraft’s intake, it gives the nose something of a whale shark’s profile.

Despite being designed to take off and land vertically from a tail-sitting position, X-BAT 001 is shown resting horizontally on ground supports. Shield AI has not explained that presentation. The footage does not show the aircraft being raised into its launch position or demonstrate its landing arrangement.

Shield AI X-BAT – everything you need to know about the AI-powered fighter jet Shield AI X-BAT – everything you need to know about the AI-powered fighter jet

X-BAT’s F110 engine appears to be installed

The video gives particular attention to the aircraft’s rear, including close-ups of a circular exhaust nozzle with overlapping metallic petals.

The assembly appears consistent with the GE F110 propulsion system selected for X-BAT. Its position suggests that propulsion hardware has been fitted to the airframe, although the footage alone cannot establish whether the complete engine installation is operational.

Shield AI’s chosen powerplant combines the F110-GE-129E with GE’s Axisymmetric Vectoring Exhaust Nozzle, or AVEN. The nozzle redirects engine thrust to provide the control needed for vertical flight.

In July, the companies announced successful integration, actuation and engine light-off testing at GE’s Peebles facility in Ohio. Those tests brought the engine, nozzle and controls together ahead of installation and flight testing on X-BAT.

The new footage shows no engine run or nozzle movement, but provides a much closer view of the hardware associated with the aircraft’s unusual takeoff and landing concept.

When will X-BAT fly?

Shield AI’s latest published schedule calls for flight testing to begin before the end of 2026. Its October update said flight-test aircraft were under construction and that weapons-bay aerodynamics had been evaluated in low- and high-speed wind-tunnel tests.

Speaking to Defense One in October, aircraft chief Armor Harris said two full-scale prototypes were being built, with initial flying focused on vertical takeoff and landing tests. He described an early operational capability around 2029 as the objective of a potential subsequent development phase.

Development flying will be based at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas. Shield AI has designated Des Moines, Washington, as X-BAT’s production location, with manufacturing planned to begin in 2029 and reach full rate in the early 2030s.

For now, X-BAT 001’s appearance offers a tangible glimpse of that ambition. The next milestone will be demonstrating that the aircraft can lift off, remain controlled in vertical flight and land safely.

 the chat header), and "height:auto" overrode that sizing and let them
 balloon to full intrinsic size. The real, measured CLS cause is the font
 swap handled above; any genuinely-unsized content image should get
 width/height attributes on the tag itself, not a blanket src selector. */
 /* Homepage auto-playing chat demo: the typing animation appends message
 bubbles and result cards, which used to GROW the demo window and push
 everything below it on every cycle (measured: CLS 0.258 on the
 homepage). Fixed internal heights make the animation play inside a
 constant-size box — newest messages stick to the bottom like a real
 chat, the results tray keeps its space reserved. */
 #lh-demo-chat {

 justify-content: flex-end;
 overflow: hidden;
 }

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.

 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {

 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {

 justify-content: flex-end;

 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {

 ];

 fd.append('page', String(page));
 fd.append('per_page', String(per_page));
 // include client-side filter selections (comma-separated slugs)

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
